domain.title: Languages & Runtimes
domain.tag: memory models · type systems · compilers · GC · concurrency
domain.why: Most people learn a programming language by memorizing which keywords to type. That gets you writing code that works. What separates someone who's just using a language from someone who understands it is knowing what's happening underneath — why a program sometimes pauses to clean up memory it isn't using, why sharing data between two parts of a program can go wrong, why some operations are fast and others are secretly slow. This domain is about seeing past the syntax to the machine underneath.

sections.t: Memory models — the part almost everyone gets wrong

concepts.t: What a memory model actually specifies
concepts.L1: Not how memory is laid out. It specifies which writes by one thread are visible to reads by another, and in what order. It is a contract between you, the compiler, and the hardware — all three of which reorder your code.
concepts.L2: People think 'memory model' means the heap/stack diagram. It means the concurrency visibility contract. Getting this wrong in an interview is instantly legible.
concepts.L3: Three agents reorder the program and the model constrains all three. The compiler may keep `payload` in a register, hoist the load of `payload` above the spin loop (it is not atomic, so the compiler assumes no other thread writes it), or sink the store. The CPU retires the store to `ready` through the store buffer and may make it globally visible before `payload`. The cache system delivers lines in whatever order coherence traffic resolves. `memory_order_release` on the store forbids the compiler and CPU from moving prior writes after it; the paired acquire forbids later reads from moving before it. Delete either annotation and every visible failure is legal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Thread A executes `payload = {v}; ready = 1;` with plain non-atomic stores. Thread B spins until `ready == 1`, then reads `payload`. Name the two independent agents that can make B read 0, and give one concrete transformation each performs.
L4.answer: Compiler and CPU. Compiler: it may reorder the two independent stores, or hoist B's load of `payload` out of the spin loop into a register before the loop, since a non-atomic object cannot legally change under it. CPU: the store to `ready` can drain from A's store buffer to coherent memory before the store to `payload`, so B observes ready==1 with payload still 0.
L4.explanation: The cache is not one of the answers - coherence guarantees all cores agree on each line's value eventually, it says nothing about the order of two different lines. Naming the store buffer and compiler-hoisting separately is the whole point of the concept.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain in two sentences why 'the memory model' is not the same question as 'where does this object live in memory'.
L4.answer: Object layout is about addresses and storage duration; a memory model is a visibility and ordering contract between threads. It states which writes a read may observe, given the synchronisation edges the program established.
L4.explanation: Layout is decided by the ABI and the allocator. Ordering is decided by the language's concurrency model plus the hardware's.

concepts.t: Sequential consistency and why nobody gives it to you
concepts.L1: SC means all threads observe one single interleaving of all operations. It is the intuitive model and no mainstream hardware or compiler provides it by default, because enforcing it forbids optimizations worth large constant factors.
concepts.L2: x86 is often described as 'strongly ordered' and people conclude it's sequentially consistent. It is not — x86-TSO permits store-load reordering via the store buffer, which is exactly the reordering that breaks Dekker's algorithm.
concepts.L3: SC requires a single global interleaving consistent with each thread's program order. To provide it, every store would have to be globally visible before the next instruction retires, which means draining the store buffer at each store - roughly a full fence per store. Measured cost on x86 is tens of cycles per store versus one. So hardware defines weaker models (x86-TSO: only store->load may reorder; ARMv8/POWER: nearly everything may reorder) and compilers do the same, since register allocation, CSE and loop-invariant hoisting are all reorderings. SC is recovered only where the programmer asks for it, at that price.

L4.prompt_tpl: x and y start at 0. T1: `x = 1; r1 = y;` T2: `y = 1; r2 = x;` (all plain int accesses, compiled -O0 for x86-64). Which of these pairs (r1,r2) can be observed: (0,1), (1,0), (1,1), (0,0)?
L4.answer: All four, including (0,0)
L4.explanation: (0,1) and (1,0) and (1,1) are all SC-legal interleavings. (0,0) is not SC-legal but is permitted by x86-TSO: each core's store sits in its own store buffer while its load of the other variable is satisfied from memory. -O0 does not save you; this is hardware, not the compiler.
options: All four, including (0,0)
(0,1), (1,0) and (1,1) only - (0,0) would need a store reordered after a load, which x86 does not do
(0,1) and (1,0) only - one thread's two statements must both complete before the other's begin

L4.prompt_tpl: Someone says 'x86 is strongly ordered, so I do not need atomics for a {n}-thread flag handshake.' Rebut in one sentence with the specific reordering x86 permits.
L4.answer: x86-TSO still permits store-to-load reordering through the per-core store buffer, so a later load can be satisfied before an earlier store is globally visible - which is exactly the reordering a flag handshake depends on not happening.
L4.explanation: x86 forbids store-store, load-load and load-store reordering. Store-load is the one it permits, and it is the one Dekker-style handshakes need.

concepts.L1: A partial order, not a temporal one. Program order within a thread, plus synchronization edges (unlock→lock, volatile write→volatile read, thread start, thread join) compose transitively. Data race = two accesses, at least one a write, not ordered by happens-before.
concepts.L2: Happens-before does not mean 'happened earlier in wall-clock time.' Two operations can be temporally ordered and still racy.
concepts.L3: Happens-before is the transitive closure of two relations: program order inside one thread, and synchronises-with edges between threads. It is a partial order, so two operations in different threads with no connecting edge are simply unordered - the model then permits a read to return either value, and the compiler is licensed to act as if the other thread does not exist. This is why adding a print statement or a sleep "fixes" a race: it perturbs timing but adds no edge, so the program is still wrong. Only an actual edge (lock, volatile, start/join, atomic release/acquire) changes what is legal.

L4.prompt_tpl: Thread A: `config = new Config(); initialised = true;` Thread B: `while (!initialised) Thread.sleep({ms}); use(config);` Both fields are plain. B eventually sees initialised == true in testing. Is the program correct? Justify with happens-before.
L4.answer: No. sleep creates no synchronises-with edge, so there is no happens-before between A's write of config and B's read of it. B may observe initialised == true and config == null, or a partially constructed Config. Making both fields volatile (or publishing through a lock) creates the edge.
L4.explanation: Timing is not ordering. The sleep only changes the probability of observing the bug, and the compiler is still free to hoist B's read of `initialised` out of the loop entirely, making it hang.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give a pair of operations that are ordered in wall-clock time but NOT ordered by happens-before, and say what the model permits as a result.
L4.answer: Thread A writes a plain field at t=0; thread B reads it at t=1 with no lock, volatile or atomic between them. Wall-clock ordered, happens-before unordered, so B is permitted to read the stale pre-write value indefinitely.
L4.explanation: Happens-before is derived from program structure and synchronisation edges, never from timestamps. Two plain writes on different threads can be seconds apart on the wall clock and still be a data race, because nothing in the program creates an edge between them.

concepts.L1: Release on a store publishes everything sequenced before it; acquire on a load subscribes to everything the matching release published. Relaxed guarantees atomicity only — no ordering. seq_cst adds a single total order across all seq_cst operations, and costs a fence.
concepts.L2: Release/acquire is a pairwise contract between a specific store and a specific load on the same variable. It does not create global ordering, and reasoning about it as though it does produces subtly wrong lock-free code.
concepts.L3: Release is a one-way barrier: nothing sequenced before it may move after it, but later operations may move before it. Acquire is the mirror. A release store and an acquire load on the same atomic object form a synchronises-with edge only when the load actually reads the value that store wrote (or a value later in that object's modification order via a release sequence). seq_cst additionally enrols the operation in one global total order shared with all other seq_cst operations, which on x86 costs a store-buffer drain on stores and on ARM costs a two-way barrier. Relaxed guarantees only that the operation is indivisible and that a single object's modification order is respected.

L4.prompt_tpl: A shared counter is incremented by {n} threads and read only after all threads join. Which memory_order is sufficient for the increment, and what would seq_cst buy you?
L4.answer: memory_order_relaxed: the read-modify-write is still indivisible, and join() supplies the happens-before edge before the final read
L4.explanation: Relaxed still guarantees the RMW is indivisible, so no increments are lost. Ordering matters only when the atomic is used to publish other state.
options: memory_order_relaxed: the read-modify-write is still indivisible, and join() supplies the happens-before edge before the final read
memory_order_seq_cst: without it two threads can read the same old value and one increment is lost
memory_order_acq_rel: each increment must publish the preceding increment to the next thread that increments

L4.prompt_tpl: Thread 1: `a.store(1, release);` Thread 2: `b.store(1, release);` Thread 3: `if (a.load(acquire)) assert(b.load(acquire) == 1);`. The author claims release/acquire gives a global order so the assert holds. Where is the error?
L4.answer: Release/acquire is pairwise between one store and the load that reads it on the SAME object. It creates no order between the store to `a` and the store to `b`, which are on different objects and in different threads, so thread 3 may see a==1 and b==0. Only seq_cst on all four operations gives the single total order that would forbid it.
L4.explanation: This is the independent-reads-of-independent-writes shape. Reasoning about acquire/release as if it were global ordering is the single most common source of wrong lock-free code.

concepts.L1: The hardware reason store-load reordering exists. A core retires a store into its own buffer and continues; other cores don't see it until it drains. mfence (or a locked instruction) drains it, which is why seq_cst stores are expensive on x86 and loads are free.
concepts.L2: The asymmetry — cheap seq_cst loads, expensive seq_cst stores on x86, roughly the inverse on ARM — is why portable lock-free code has such different performance profiles across architectures.
concepts.L3: A store first retires into the core's private store buffer so the pipeline need not wait for the cache line's exclusive ownership, which can cost hundreds of cycles. Loads snoop the local store buffer (store-to-load forwarding), so a core always sees its own stores in order - which is why single-threaded code is unaffected. Other cores see the store only when it drains to L1 and coherence propagates it. That gap is exactly store-load reordering. mfence, or any lock-prefixed instruction such as xchg or lock add, stalls until the buffer drains, which is why a seq_cst store costs ~20-40 cycles and a seq_cst load costs zero on x86.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64, a loop performs {n} seq_cst atomic stores. Rewritten with release stores it performs the same {n} stores. Which version has more instructions of ordering cost, and roughly what is the per-operation difference in cycles?
L4.answer: The seq_cst version. Release stores are plain mov (no ordering cost); seq_cst stores compile to a locked xchg or mov+mfence costing roughly 20-40 cycles each, so the difference is about 20-40 cycles per store.
L4.explanation: Exact cost is microarchitecture-dependent - measure it - but the order of magnitude is tens of cycles, not one and not thousands.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86 seq_cst loads are free and seq_cst stores are expensive. On AArch64 the balance is different. Explain the asymmetry and what it means for portable lock-free code.
L4.answer: x86-TSO already forbids every reordering except store-load, so only the store side needs a fence. AArch64 permits load-load and store-store reordering too, so seq_cst is implemented with ldar/stlr - cost lands on both sides, and loads are no longer free. Portable lock-free code therefore has a different hot path on each architecture, and a design tuned to make loads cheap on x86 can be the wrong shape on ARM.
L4.explanation: This is why benchmarks of lock-free structures do not transfer across ISAs, and why read-mostly designs look better on x86 than they do on ARM servers.

concepts.t: Cache coherence is not memory ordering
concepts.L1: MESI guarantees that all cores eventually agree on the value of each cache line individually. It says nothing about the relative order of operations on different lines. Coherence is per-location; consistency is across locations.
concepts.L2: Very common conflation. 'The caches are coherent so I don't need barriers' is wrong, and it's wrong for a reason you can state precisely.
concepts.L3: MESI serialises accesses to a single line: to write, a core must obtain the line in Modified state, which invalidates every other copy, so all writes to that line form one total order every core agrees on. Nothing in the protocol relates a write to line X with a write to line Y. Cores also buffer coherence work: invalidate messages sit in invalidation queues and are acknowledged before being applied, and stores wait in store buffers before entering the protocol at all. Both queues are outside coherence's guarantee. Barriers exist precisely to flush them, which is why "the caches are coherent" never implies "I need no barriers".

L4.prompt_tpl: True or false, and justify: 'Because the hardware keeps caches coherent, two threads reading two different atomic variables will always agree on which was updated first.'
L4.answer: False: coherence orders accesses to each line independently and says nothing about the relative order of updates to two different lines
L4.explanation: The IRIW litmus test makes this concrete: on POWER, two reader threads can genuinely observe the two writes in opposite orders.
options: False: coherence orders accesses to each line independently and says nothing about the relative order of updates to two different lines
True: a coherent cache serialises every write into one global order that all cores observe
False for plain variables, but true for std::atomic: any two atomic loads are guaranteed to agree on the order regardless of memory_order

L4.prompt_tpl: State in one sentence each what MESI guarantees and what it does not.
L4.answer: It guarantees that a cache line is never writable in two caches at once and that all cores eventually agree on a single order of writes to that one line. It does not guarantee anything about the order in which one core's writes to different lines become visible to another core - that is the memory model's job, and it is enforced with fences, not with coherence.
L4.explanation: Coherence is per-location; consistency is across locations. Almost every wrong intuition about memory models comes from applying a per-line guarantee across lines. Store buffers and invalidation queues sit between the core and the coherent cache, and they are what the fences drain.

concepts.L1: volatile gives release on write and acquire on read plus seq_cst ordering among volatiles. final fields get a freeze at constructor exit guaranteeing safe publication — provided 'this' does not escape the constructor. Data races are not undefined behavior in Java; they yield out-of-thin-air-restricted but weird values.
concepts.L2: The final-field guarantee is why immutable objects are safely publishable without synchronization — and it is silently void if the constructor leaks 'this' to another thread.
concepts.L3: JSR-133 defines the freeze action at the end of a constructor for every final field. A thread that reads a reference to the object through any path - even a data race - is guaranteed to see the final fields at their frozen values, because the JIT and the hardware are forbidden from reordering the final-field writes past the constructor's end. This costs a StoreStore barrier at constructor exit on weak hardware and nothing on x86. If the constructor publishes `this` before that point, another thread can hold the reference before the freeze and observe default values. Non-final, non-volatile fields get no such guarantee at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: A class with only final fields registers itself in a static listener map from inside its constructor: `Registry.add(this);` on the last line. The author says immutability makes it thread-safe. What breaks?
L4.answer: Publishing `this` inside the constructor happens before the final-field freeze, so another thread that pulls the object out of the registry can observe the final fields at their default values (null/0). The fix is a static factory that constructs first and registers after the constructor returns.
L4.explanation: Immutability gives safe publication only via the freeze at constructor exit. Escaping `this` moves the publication earlier than the freeze, and the guarantee evaporates silently - it will pass every test on x86.

L4.prompt_tpl: In C++ a data race is undefined behaviour. In Java it is not. What does Java give you instead, and why did it have to?
L4.answer: Java guarantees no out-of-thin-air values: a race yields some value actually written by some thread, and memory safety and type safety survive. It had to, because the JVM is a sandbox - allowing UB would let racy untrusted bytecode forge pointers and break the security model.
L4.explanation: The cost is that the JMM's formal specification is far harder than C++'s, and the out-of-thin-air prohibition still has no fully satisfactory formalisation.

concepts.L1: A data race in C++ is undefined behavior, full stop. This is why the compiler is allowed to assume single-threaded semantics for non-atomic accesses, and why 'it worked in debug' means nothing.
concepts.L2: The consequence people miss: UB is not 'unpredictable value', it's 'the entire program has no defined meaning', including time-travel effects where the compiler deletes a check that precedes the racy access.
concepts.L3: Because non-atomic objects cannot legally change under it, the compiler treats them as single-threaded. It will hoist a load out of a loop into a register, split one source-level store into two machine stores, or invent a speculative store to a location it proved it would write on some path. Any of these turns a benign-looking race into a value no thread ever wrote. UB is worse still than a wrong value: the standard imposes no requirement on the whole execution, so a compiler that derives a contradiction from an assumed-impossible path may delete the branch that leads to it - including checks written before the offending line, since it can prove control never legally reaches them.

L4.prompt_tpl: `int *p = get(); int x = *p; if (p == nullptr) return {r}; return x;` compiled at -O2. What can the compiler do with the null check, and why?
L4.answer: Delete it. The dereference on the previous line is UB if p is null, so the compiler may assume p is non-null from that point on - and, since the assumption holds at the dereference, the later comparison is provably false and the branch is dead code.
L4.explanation: This is the standard time-travel shape. Order the check before the dereference and the deletion becomes illegal.

L4.prompt_tpl: 'It works in debug builds' is offered as evidence a racy program is fine. Give the two independent reasons that is not evidence.
L4.answer: First, -O0 suppresses the compiler-side transformations (hoisting, register caching) but not the hardware reordering, so the race is still live. Second, UB means the program has no defined meaning at any optimisation level; a build that happens to work is a coincidence the standard does not renew.
L4.explanation: Use -fsanitize=thread instead: TSan tracks happens-before edges at runtime and reports the race rather than the symptom.

concepts.L1: The canonical example. Broken without volatile because the constructor's writes can be reordered after the reference publication, so another thread sees a non-null reference to a partially constructed object.
concepts.L2: Java fixed this in JSR-133 (Java 5) via volatile semantics. Many engineers learned it was 'broken' and never learned it was fixed, or why.
concepts.L3: `instance = new Resource()` is three steps: allocate, run the constructor, publish the reference. Steps 2 and 3 are independent for a compiler that does not model other threads, so it may publish first and initialise after. A second thread taking the fast path then sees a non-null reference and returns an object whose fields are still zero. Declaring the field volatile makes the publishing write a release, forbidding the constructor's writes from sinking past it, and makes the fast-path read an acquire that subscribes to them. In C++ the same fix is `std::atomic<T*>` with release/acquire, or simply a function-local static, whose initialisation the standard requires to be thread-safe.

L4.prompt_tpl: A codebase has double-checked locking with a plain (non-volatile) static field and {n} years of production uptime on x86 servers. Is it correct? What changes if it is deployed on ARM?
L4.answer: Not correct - it is broken by the model even if it has never failed. x86-TSO forbids store-store reordering so the hardware will not expose it, but the JIT is still allowed to sink the constructor's writes past the publication. On ARM the hardware permits the reordering too, so the failure becomes reachable in practice.
L4.explanation: Uptime is not a proof. This is the classic case of a bug that surfaces only on migration to weaker hardware.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give the Java idiom that achieves the same lazy singleton with no volatile and no synchronized on the fast path, and say what makes it safe.
L4.answer: The lazy holder: a private static nested class whose static field holds the instance. The JVM's class initialisation lock guarantees the holder class is initialised exactly once, and class initialisation provides the happens-before edge, so the fast path is a plain static field read.
L4.explanation: Class initialisation semantics (JLS 12.4.2) give you laziness and safe publication for free. Prefer it; reach for double-checked locking only when the instance is per-object rather than per-class.

concepts.L1: A data race is unsynchronised conflicting access to one location - a memory-model violation, and UB in C and C++. A race condition is a correctness bug whose outcome depends on timing. Neither implies the other.
concepts.L2: Removing every data race does not make a program correct. Wrapping each individual access in a lock leaves check-then-act intact: the invariant spans two critical sections, so the window merely moved. TSan finds data races and is silent on this entire class.
concepts.L3: The distinction is which contract is broken. A data race breaks the language's memory model, so the compiler's single-threaded assumptions become false and the program has no defined meaning - the failure can be a torn value, an invented value, or deleted code. A race condition breaks your invariant while every individual operation behaves exactly as specified; the machine did what you asked, and what you asked was wrong. This is why the remedies differ: data races are fixed by adding synchronisation to each access, race conditions by widening the critical section until it covers the whole invariant, or by switching to an atomic compound operation such as a CAS or a conditional update.

L4.prompt_tpl: `if (map.containsKey(k)) return map.get(k); else {{ v = compute(); map.put(k, v); return v; }}` on a ConcurrentHashMap with {t} threads. Is there a data race? Is there a race condition? What is the fix?
L4.answer: No data race: ConcurrentHashMap synchronises each operation internally. There is a race condition: two threads can both find the key absent and both compute and put, so compute() runs twice and one result is discarded. The fix is one atomic compound operation, computeIfAbsent.
L4.explanation: A thread-safe collection makes each call atomic, never a sequence of calls. This is the single most common misuse of concurrent containers.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team runs TSan clean on a service that still corrupts state under load. What class of bug remains, and what tool or technique would you use instead?
L4.answer: Race conditions - invariants spanning multiple correctly synchronised operations. TSan verifies happens-before between memory accesses and can say nothing about whether your critical sections cover the right span. Reach for invariant assertions under the lock, a model checker (loom, TLA+), or deterministic interleaving tests.
L4.explanation: TSan clean means the memory model is satisfied. It is a necessary condition and nowhere near a sufficient one.

concepts.t: volatile is not atomic (except in Java, where it is not volatile)
concepts.L1: C and C++ volatile constrains the compiler's treatment of one access - no elision, no merging, no reordering with other volatile accesses - and emits no fences. It is for MMIO and signal handlers. Java's volatile is an entirely different keyword that does give ordering.
concepts.L2: The name is shared and the semantics are not, so C programmers who learned Java's volatile write racy flag code that appears to work on x86 because the hardware already forbids the reorderings that would expose it. volatile int x; x++ is still three instructions and still loses updates.
concepts.L3: In C and C++ a volatile access is an observable side effect of the abstract machine, so the compiler must emit exactly the loads and stores you wrote, in their relative order, and may not cache the value in a register. That is the whole guarantee. It emits no barrier, so the CPU may still reorder a volatile store against an ordinary load, and a volatile int on a machine without a single-instruction access may still tear. Java, by contrast, defines volatile in terms of the memory model: a write is a release, a read is an acquire, and all volatile operations share a total order - which the JIT implements with real fences. Same spelling, disjoint contracts.

L4.prompt_tpl: A worker loops on `while (!stop) work();` with `volatile bool stop` set by another thread, and `volatile int processed; processed++;` as a counter. Which part is defensible and which is broken?
L4.answer: The stop flag is defensible in practice - volatile stops the compiler hoisting the load out of the loop, and a bool store is single-instruction on every real target - but it is still formally a data race and std::atomic<bool> with relaxed ordering is the correct spelling and costs the same. The counter is broken: ++ is load-add-store, volatile makes none of it atomic, and increments are lost.
L4.explanation: This is the exact split that makes volatile so durable a mistake: the flag half usually works, so the counter half inherits its credibility.

L4.prompt_tpl: Name the two cases where volatile is the right keyword in C, and say why std::atomic would be wrong there.
L4.answer: Memory-mapped I/O registers, where each read and write must actually occur and must not be merged or reordered with other device accesses; and a variable written by a signal handler and read by the interrupted code (volatile sig_atomic_t). std::atomic would add unnecessary synchronisation and, for MMIO, may not preserve access width or count - and for the signal case the ordering is within one thread, so no inter-thread machinery is wanted.
L4.explanation: Both cases are about the compiler's model of observable effects, not about threads. That is what volatile was designed for.

# C is {{c3::static}} and {{c4::weak}}.
# JavaScript is dynamic and weak: "1" + 1 evaluates to {{c5::"11"}}.

concepts.L1: Static/dynamic is about when types are checked. Strong/weak is about whether the language will silently reinterpret a value. Python is dynamic and strong. C is static and weak.
concepts.L2: These get collapsed constantly. Naming them as orthogonal is a cheap but real signal.
concepts.L3: The axes are independent because they answer different questions. Static/dynamic asks when the checker runs: before execution over all paths (conservative, rejects some correct programs) or at each operation over the actual value (permissive, finds errors only on executed paths). Strong/weak asks what the checker does with a mismatch: refuse, or coerce by reinterpreting the bits or the value. C's implicit integer conversions and its permission to cast any object pointer to any other are weakness inside a static system. Python raises TypeError on `"1" + 1` at run time - that is strength inside a dynamic one.

L4.prompt_tpl: Place these four on both axes: C, Python, Java, JavaScript. Justify the two that surprise people.
L4.answer: C static/weak; Python dynamic/strong; Java static/mostly strong; JavaScript dynamic/weak. The surprises: Python is strong despite being dynamic (it refuses "1" + 1), and C is weak despite being static (unsigned conversions and pointer casts reinterpret silently).
L4.explanation: Java is 'mostly' strong because it still permits unchecked casts and silent widening; strength is a spectrum, staticness is closer to binary.

L4.prompt_tpl: In C, `unsigned u = {n}; if (u > -1) puts("yes"); else puts("no");` What prints, and which axis explains it?
L4.answer: no. The usual arithmetic conversions convert -1 to UINT_MAX before the comparison, so u > -1 is false for any u. This is weak typing inside a static system.
L4.explanation: The comparison typechecks fine - that is staticness doing its job. The silent reinterpretation of -1 as a huge unsigned is weakness. -Wsign-compare warns.

Erasure preserves the theorem only if you cannot recover the type - reflection, instanceof and unchecked casts all break it, which is why Java's `List<String>` can be made to hold an Integer. C++ templates never had it: each instantiation is typechecked after substitution, so `t.foo()` in the body is legal for any T that happens to have foo.

L4.answer: Exactly one for a -> a (the identity). For length-n lists mapped to length-n lists, n^n functions if repetition is allowed (each output slot picks one input index), of which n! are permutations.
L4.explanation: The a -> a case is the cleanest demonstration of parametricity: nothing can be done with a value of unknown type except return it.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Java method takes `List<{T}>` and stores it in an `Object[]`, later retrieving and casting. It compiles with an unchecked warning and throws ClassCastException in production. Explain in terms of erasure.
L4.answer: At run time the list has no element type - the parameter is erased to List - so nothing checks what was inserted. The cast the compiler inserted at the retrieval site is the first check, and it fires far from the offending insertion. That is exactly parametricity lost: run-time code can observe and violate the type argument.
L4.explanation: Heap pollution. The unchecked warning is the compiler telling you it can no longer guarantee the invariant.

concepts.L1: Covariance, contravariance, invariance. A function type is contravariant in its argument and covariant in its return. Mutable containers must be invariant, which is why Java's covariant arrays require a runtime store check and can throw ArrayStoreException.
concepts.L2: Java arrays are covariant and this was a known-unsound design decision made deliberately before generics existed. Being able to explain why it's unsound is a strong signal.
concepts.L3: Subtyping is substitutability: S <: T means an S is usable wherever a T is required. For a read-only container that holds T, every read yields a T, so Box[S] <: Box[T] is sound - covariance. For a write-only sink, every write supplies a T, so the direction flips - contravariance. A mutable container is both a source and a sink, so both directions must hold simultaneously, which forces equality: invariance. Java chose covariant arrays in 1.0 because without generics there was no other way to write a polymorphic sort, and paid for it with a store check on every array write plus a run-time exception class that exists solely to report the unsoundness.

L4.prompt_tpl: `Object[] a = new {S}[{n}]; a[0] = new Object();` What happens, at which phase, and why was the language designed to allow the first line?
L4.answer: Compiles; throws ArrayStoreException at run time on the assignment. The first line is allowed because Java 1.0 made arrays covariant so that methods like sort(Object[]) could be applied to any array, there being no generics to express it otherwise.
L4.explanation: Every aastore in the JVM carries this check. It is a permanent per-write cost paid by all Java array code to support a knowingly unsound rule.

L4.explanation: Java does not express this in the type Function<T,R> itself - you need `Function<? super Dog, ? extends Animal>` at the use site.

No: Java generics are invariant, so no Function type is ever a subtype of another Function type

concepts.L2: The tradeoff is the interesting part: inference power and type system expressiveness are in direct tension, and every language picks a point on that curve.

Generalisation happens only at let, which is what makes `id` usable at two types in one scope while a lambda-bound variable stays monomorphic. The system is decidable and principal - there is a single most general type - because the constraint language is equality only. Introduce subtyping and constraints become inequalities over a lattice, so the solver must choose among incomparable solutions; introduce rank-2 polymorphism and even checking becomes undecidable. Hence Java's annotations at every method boundary.

L4.answer: ML's constraints are pure equalities over type variables, so unification yields a principal type. Java added subtyping (constraints become bounds, and there is no single best solution) and later erased generics with wildcards, so inference is deliberately local: it solves for type arguments at a call site but never for a declaration's parameter types.

concepts.L1: Sum types plus product types plus pattern matching with compiler-checked exhaustiveness. The reason Rust and ML-family code has fewer 'unhandled case' bugs is structural, not cultural.
concepts.L2: Option/Maybe is not primarily about null safety — it's about making the absence case unignorable at the type level. The nullability is incidental.
concepts.L3: The type is a tagged union: a discriminant plus a payload sized to the largest variant, so `match` is a jump on the tag and the compiler statically knows the complete set of tags. Exhaustiveness checking is then a covering problem over that finite set, which the compiler solves with the usefulness algorithm (Maranget). The engineering consequence is a change-detection mechanism: adding a variant turns every incomplete match into a compile error, giving you a worklist of exactly the sites that need attention. A catch-all arm converts that compile error into a silent run-time fallthrough, which is why `_` in a match on a domain enum is usually a bug in waiting.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team adds a {v}th variant to a Rust enum used in {n} places. Half the match sites end with `_ => default()`. What does the compiler report, and what is the real cost of the catch-all arms?
L4.answer: Only the match sites without a catch-all fail to compile. The catch-all sites compile and silently route the new variant to default(), so the compiler's change-detection is exactly the half you disabled - the bug ships in the arms you thought were the safe ones.
L4.explanation: Reserve `_` for genuinely open sets (parsing bytes, external protocol codes) and enumerate variants for closed domain types.

L4.prompt_tpl: 'Option exists to avoid null pointer exceptions.' Sharpen that claim.
L4.answer: Option's contribution is that absence is a distinct constructor, so the type of a possibly-absent T is different from T and every use site must handle both cases before it can touch the value. Null-safety follows from that; it is a consequence, not the mechanism. A nullable reference has the same run-time representation and no such obligation.
L4.explanation: Rust exploits this: Option<&T> is niche-optimised to the same size as &T, since the null bit pattern is unused. Zero cost, total checking.

concepts.L1: Values used exactly once (linear) or at most once (affine). Rust's ownership is affine typing with borrowing. This is what allows compile-time memory safety without a GC.
concepts.L2: Rust's borrow checker is usually described as a safety feature. It's more precisely a static approximation of aliasing and lifetime, and the restriction 'one mutable reference or many shared' is exactly the condition that makes data races statically impossible.
concepts.L3: "One mutable reference xor many shared references" is precisely the condition under which no two threads, and no two code paths, can hold a writable alias to the same object at once. A data race requires two accesses to the same location with at least one write and no ordering - the first clause is unsatisfiable if a writable alias is unique. So Rust does not detect races; it makes them unrepresentable in safe code, and the borrow checker is the static approximation that decides it. Being an approximation, it rejects sound programs (a self-referential struct, a doubly linked list), which is why unsafe, Cell/RefCell and Pin exist as escape hatches.

L4.prompt_tpl: `let mut v = vec![{a}, {b}]; let first = &v[0]; v.push({c}); println!("{{}}", first);` Why is this rejected, and what real bug does the rejection prevent?
L4.answer: push needs &mut v while the shared borrow `first` is still live, violating the aliasing rule. The real bug: push may reallocate the buffer, leaving `first` dangling - the classic iterator-invalidation use-after-free that C++ compiles happily.
L4.explanation: Note the borrow checker is not reasoning about reallocation. It rejects the alias, and dangling-freedom falls out.

L4.prompt_tpl: Rust is affine rather than linear. Give a concrete consequence of that choice.
L4.answer: Values may be discarded without being used, so a Result can be ignored (only a lint complains) and a MutexGuard can simply be dropped. A truly linear system would force every value to be consumed exactly once, which would make early return and panic unwinding far harder to express.
L4.explanation: std::mem::forget and Box::leak are the deliberate holes: Rust does not even guarantee destructors run, which is why leak-safety is not part of the soundness contract.

L4.prompt_tpl: Under Curry-Howard, what program corresponds to the proposition A -> (B -> A)?

L4.prompt_tpl: Name one shipped system whose correctness is machine-checked with dependent types, and say what was actually proved.

concepts.L1: TypeScript, mypy, Sorbet. The hard problem is the boundary: sound gradual typing requires runtime contracts at the typed/untyped border, which is expensive, so most practical systems are unsound by design.
concepts.L2: TypeScript is explicitly unsound — bivariant method parameters, any, type assertions. Knowing that it chose developer experience over soundness deliberately is more useful than treating unsoundness as a bug.
concepts.L3: Soundness at the boundary requires a wrapper: when a typed function receives an untyped value it must check it, and a higher-order value must be wrapped in a proxy that checks each later call, with blame tracking to name the guilty party. Takikawa et al. measured this in Typed Racket and found slowdowns up to two orders of magnitude on partially typed configurations - the boundary crossings, not the checks themselves, dominate. So TypeScript and mypy erase types instead: zero run-time cost, no guarantee. Knowing that unsoundness is the deliberate price of the erasure is the difference between using the tool and complaining about it.

L4.prompt_tpl: TypeScript: `const xs: number[] = JSON.parse('["a","b"]'); console.log(xs[0].toFixed({d}));` Does it compile? What happens at run time?

L4.explanation: This is the boundary in miniature. Typing the parse result as `unknown` and narrowing with a validator (zod, io-ts, a hand-written guard) is the fix; `any` is the hole.

L4.prompt_tpl: Is TypeScript's unsoundness a bug to be fixed? Argue the actual design position in three sentences.
L4.answer: No - it is a stated non-goal in the design guidelines. Sound gradual typing costs run-time contracts and rejects large amounts of idiomatic JavaScript, and TypeScript's purpose is to type existing JS with zero run-time footprint. The honest framing is that it is a very good bug-finder and a very poor proof.
L4.explanation: Knowing bivariant method parameters, `any`, and unchecked assertions are the three named holes - and that each buys ergonomics - is what separates informed use from cargo cult.

concepts.t: Static and dynamic dispatch: vtables, fat pointers, monomorphisation
concepts.L1: Static dispatch resolves the callee at compile time, so it can be inlined; dynamic dispatch loads the target from a table at run time. C++ and Java put the pointer in the object; Rust and Go put it in the reference, as a fat pointer beside the data pointer.
concepts.L2: The cost of a virtual call is not the two loads. It is that the optimiser cannot see through it, so inlining, constant propagation and escape analysis all stop at the call. Rust's `impl Trait` and `dyn Trait` differ in exactly that, not in call overhead.
concepts.L3: Under the Itanium C++ ABI, each polymorphic class has one static vtable and each object stores a pointer to it at offset 0, so the call is two dependent loads plus an indirect branch; both usually hit, so the direct cost is small. Rust separates the vtable from the object, so a value only pays for dynamic dispatch where a `dyn` reference is formed, which is why a Vec<Circle> has no per-element overhead while a Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> has a pointer and a vtable pointer per element plus a heap allocation. Monomorphisation removes the indirection completely at the cost of one code copy per instantiated type - the reason Rust and C++ binaries grow with generic use.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64: what is sizeof for `struct A {{ int x; }}` and `struct B {{ virtual ~B(); int x; }}`, and what is size_of::<&dyn Trait>() versus size_of::<&{T}>() in Rust?
L4.answer: sizeof(A) == 4. sizeof(B) == 16: an 8-byte vptr, then int x, then 4 bytes of padding to keep alignment 8. In Rust, &dyn Trait is 16 bytes (data pointer plus vtable pointer) and &T for a sized T is 8.
L4.explanation: Adding a single virtual function to a small struct can quadruple its size, which matters enormously for arrays of them - a real reason to avoid virtual on value-like types.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C++ base-class constructor calls a virtual method that the derived class overrides. The derived override never runs. Why?
L4.answer: During the base constructor the object's vptr still points at the base class vtable - the derived part is not yet constructed, so calling its override would touch uninitialised members. The base version is called instead (and if it is pure virtual, the program terminates). The same applies in destructors, in reverse.
L4.explanation: Java behaves oppositely and worse: the derived override IS called, and it observes the derived fields still at their defaults. Two languages, two wrong-looking answers, both principled.

std::vector<int> v{1,2,3};

auto& b = v[0];            // int&     - binds to the element
const auto& c = v[0];      // const int&
decltype(auto) d = v[0];   // int&     - preserves the exact declared type of the expression

var list = new ArrayList<String>();   // Java 10+: locals only, never fields or parameters

let mut xs = Vec::new();   // Rust infers Vec<i32> from the LATER push - inference is
xs.push(1i32);             // whole-function, not left-to-right

concepts.L1: auto, var and let infer a local's type from its initialiser and, in Rust, its later uses. All three stop at function boundaries: parameter and return types are annotations, because whole-program inference over subtyping and overloading is undecidable or unstable.
concepts.L2: `auto x = container[i]` silently copies, because auto strips references. For a vector<bool> it is worse: you capture the proxy object, and `auto` gives you a reference-like thing whose lifetime is tied to a temporary. Use `auto&` or `const auto&` deliberately, not by habit.
concepts.L3: C++'s `auto` is specified by reusing template argument deduction, which by design decays: array to pointer, function to pointer, reference dropped, top-level const dropped. That is why `auto x = v[0]` copies and `auto s = getString()` is fine but `auto s = obj.name()` copies a member. `decltype(auto)` exists precisely to opt out and preserve value category. Rust's inference is a constraint solver over the function body, so a variable's type may be determined by a use twenty lines later, which is why removing one line can produce an error at a completely different one. Neither system crosses a function signature: that boundary is what keeps error messages local and compilation modular.

L4.prompt_tpl: `std::map<std::string,int> m = ...; for (const auto& [k, v] : m) ...` versus `for (const std::pair<std::string,int>& p : m) ...` with {n} entries. Which one copies, and why?
L4.answer: The second copies every element. A map's value_type is pair<const string, int>, not pair<string,int>, so the reference cannot bind directly; a temporary is materialised and the const reference binds to that - once per iteration. The structured binding with auto& deduces the true type and copies nothing.
L4.explanation: This is the classic silent-copy bug that -Wrange-loop-analysis (clang) catches. Writing the type out by hand is what causes it; auto is what prevents it.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can Rust infer that `let mut v = Vec::new();` is a Vec<{T}> when the only clue appears three lines later, while C++ cannot do the same for `auto v = std::vector();`?
L4.answer: Rust type-checks a function body as one constraint system: the later push(x: T) generates a constraint that unifies with the element type of v. C++ deduction is a local, single-expression rule applied at the declaration, with no mechanism to consult later statements - so an initialiser that determines nothing is an error.
L4.explanation: This is the same expressiveness-versus-locality trade as Hindley-Milner: Rust pays with error messages that point away from the real line.

$ clang -S -emit-llvm -O0 hello.c -o -  # LLVM IR before optimisation
$ opt -O2 -print-after-all hello.ll     # every pass, and the IR after each

$ clang -mllvm -print-pipeline-passes -O2 hello.c   # the pass pipeline itself

concepts.L1: Lexing, parsing, AST, semantic analysis, IR lowering, optimization passes, instruction selection, register allocation, scheduling, emission. Modern compilers run dozens of passes over an SSA-form IR.
concepts.L2: The passes are ordered and the ordering matters enormously — inlining before or after constant propagation produces different results, and phase ordering is a genuinely unsolved problem.
concepts.L3: The front end is language-specific and the back end is target-specific; the IR in the middle is what lets LLVM support N languages and M targets with N+M components instead of N*M. Passes are ordered because each both consumes and produces facts: inlining exposes constants to propagate, constant propagation makes branches dead, dead-code elimination shrinks functions back under the inliner's size budget. The optimal order is input-dependent and searching it is intractable, so every compiler ships a hand-tuned fixed pipeline with a few repeated passes; -O3 largely means "run more of them, with bigger thresholds", not "a better algorithm".

L4.prompt_tpl: A function is {n} lines long and calls a small helper that would fold to a constant once inlined. Explain why running constant propagation before the inliner gives a worse result than after, and what that says about pass ordering.
L4.answer: Before inlining, the helper's body is behind a call boundary, so the propagator cannot see the argument is constant and folds nothing. After inlining, the argument is a literal in the caller's body and folds, possibly killing a branch. Ordering matters because passes create each other's opportunities, and no single order is best for all inputs - phase ordering is unsolved.
L4.explanation: This is why LLVM runs the inliner inside a CGSCC pass manager that re-runs the function simplification pipeline on each callee after inlining.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does LLVM's design use one IR between {n} front ends and several back ends? State the combinatorial argument.
L4.answer: With a shared IR you write N front ends plus M back ends; without one you write N*M translators. The optimiser is written once against the IR and is inherited by every language and target.
L4.explanation: The cost is that the IR must be expressive enough for all of them and specific enough to optimise - which is why LLVM IR is typed, SSA, and low-level, and why higher-level languages increasingly add their own IR above it (MLIR, Swift's SIL, Rust's MIR).

concepts.L1: Static single assignment: every variable assigned exactly once, with phi nodes at control-flow merges. Makes def-use chains explicit, which makes most dataflow optimizations dramatically simpler.
concepts.L2: Why it matters practically: nearly every optimization you'd name — constant propagation, dead code elimination, GVN — is either trivial or vastly cheaper in SSA.
concepts.L3: In non-SSA IR, asking "what defines this use?" requires a dataflow analysis over the CFG. In SSA the answer is a pointer: each use names its unique definition, so def-use chains are explicit and most analyses become graph walks rather than fixpoint iterations. Constant propagation reduces to substitution; dead-code elimination to "no uses"; GVN to hashing the defining expression. Phi placement uses Cytron's dominance-frontier algorithm, and going out of SSA replaces phis with copies on the incoming edges - where the lost-copy and swap problems live, which is why register allocators care about the exit as much as the entry.

L4.prompt_tpl: Convert to SSA: `i = 0; while (i < {n}) {{ i = i + 1; }} return i;` How many phi nodes are required and where? Answer with the number of phi nodes.
L4.answer: One, at the loop header: i2 = phi [0, entry], [i3, latch], with i3 = i2 + 1 in the body. The header is the only join point with two reaching definitions.
L4.explanation: Loop headers are the canonical phi site: the dominance frontier of the definition in the body is the header itself.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is dead code elimination nearly trivial in SSA form?
L4.answer: Because each value carries its complete use list. An instruction with no uses and no side effects is dead and can be deleted immediately, and deleting it may drop the use counts of its operands to zero, so a worklist converges without any dataflow fixpoint over the CFG.
L4.explanation: Compare the non-SSA version: you need live-variable analysis, an iterative backwards fixpoint over all blocks, before you can delete anything.

prereqs: lang:The pipeline

concepts.L1: Inlining itself saves a call. Its real value is exposing the callee's body to the caller's context, enabling constant propagation, escape analysis, and dead branch elimination across the boundary.
concepts.L2: This is why 'small functions are free' is true in practice but 'the JIT will inline it' is not a safe assumption — inlining is budget-limited by bytecode size in HotSpot, and megamorphic call sites don't inline at all.
concepts.L3: A call costs a handful of cycles - argument marshalling, the jump, the return - and modern predictors hide most of it. The real win is that the callee's body enters the caller's dataflow: an argument that is a constant at this site propagates, a branch on it dies, an object that would escape through the call is now proved local and can be scalar-replaced. That is why inlining is called the enabling optimisation: it is the precondition for the others. It is also self-limiting, since each inline grows the caller, hurts I-cache density and can spill registers, so every compiler enforces a size budget and inlines by profile where it has one.

L4.prompt_tpl: A hot Java loop calls an interface method with {k} implementing classes observed at that site. Predict inlining behaviour for k=1, k=2 and k={k}, and give the mechanism.
L4.answer: k=1 monomorphic: JIT inlines directly with a class-check guard and deoptimisation if it fails. k=2 bimorphic: two guarded inline bodies. k>=3 megamorphic: no inlining, a real vtable/itable dispatch remains, and every downstream optimisation across the boundary is lost.
L4.explanation: The degree is a property of the profile at that call site, not of the source. The same method inlined in one caller can be megamorphic in another.

L4.prompt_tpl: An engineer marks a {n}-line hot function `always_inline` and throughput drops. Give two mechanisms that explain it.
L4.answer: Instruction cache pressure: the body is duplicated at every call site, so the hot loop no longer fits in L1i and front-end stalls dominate. Register pressure: the enlarged function needs more live values than the register file provides, so the allocator spills to stack inside the loop.
L4.explanation: Inlining is a size/speed trade with a real optimum. always_inline overrides the heuristic that was measuring it.

concepts.L1: Proving an allocation doesn't outlive its frame allows stack allocation or scalar replacement — decomposing the object into registers. This is why allocation-heavy Java can outperform naive expectations.
concepts.L2: It's fragile. One path where the reference escapes kills it for all paths, and there's no reliable way to observe whether it fired without reading JIT output.
concepts.L3: The analysis computes, for each allocation, whether any reference to it can be reached after the frame dies: stored to a field of an escaping object, returned, passed to a method the compiler cannot see through, or published to another thread. If not, the object can live on the stack, or better, be scalar-replaced so its fields become SSA values in registers and the header never exists. It is a may-analysis over the merged CFG, so a single escaping path taints the allocation everywhere; inlining is its precondition, since an un-inlined callee is opaque. That fragility is the practical problem: an unrelated refactor can silently reintroduce megabytes per second of allocation.

L4.prompt_tpl: Go: `func f() *int {{ x := {n}; return &x }}`. Does x live on the stack or the heap, and what does `go build -gcflags=-m` print?
L4.answer: Heap. The compiler prints something like './main.go: moved to heap: x' because the address escapes through the return value. Go's escape analysis, not the syntax, decides stack vs heap - taking an address does not by itself force heap allocation.
L4.explanation: This is why returning a pointer to a local is safe in Go and UB in C: Go moves the object, C does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Java hot path allocated nothing per iteration; after adding `if (log.isDebugEnabled()) log.debug("v=" + v);` allocation rate jumps even with debug disabled. Explain.
L4.answer: The concatenation is an argument expression, so it is evaluated only inside the guard - but if the guard was not the change, the likelier cause is that the added call pushed the enclosing method past the inlining budget, so a previously inlined callee is now a real call, its allocation is no longer provably non-escaping, and scalar replacement is lost for the whole path.
L4.explanation: Escape analysis depends on inlining, and inlining depends on a byte-size budget. Adding code anywhere in a hot method can silently disable both. Verify with -XX:+PrintInlining rather than reasoning.

concepts.L1: Monomorphic call sites get inlined directly. Bimorphic get a type check plus two inlined bodies. Megamorphic (3+ observed types) fall back to a vtable dispatch and stop inlining.
concepts.L2: This is the concrete mechanism behind 'interfaces are slow in hot loops.' It's not the interface — it's the call site polymorphism degree, which is a profile property, not a source property.
concepts.L3: A virtual call is a load of the vtable pointer from the object, a load of the slot, and an indirect branch - perhaps 3-5 cycles when the indirect predictor hits. That is not the cost that matters. The cost is that the target is unknown, so nothing can be inlined and no analysis crosses the boundary. A JIT with a type profile can gamble: it emits a class-pointer comparison, inlines the body for the hot receiver, and installs an uncommon trap that deoptimises if a new type appears. With three or more receivers the check chain stops paying and it falls back to the vtable. AOT compilers get the same effect only via devirtualisation proofs - final, sealed, LTO whole-program analysis - or PGO.

L4.prompt_tpl: Two microbenchmarks call the same interface method {n} million times. One is 4x faster. The source is identical; only the set of objects fed in differs. Explain and name the knob you would inspect.
L4.answer: The fast one feeds a single implementation, so the call site is monomorphic and the JIT inlines through it; the slow one feeds three or more, so it is megamorphic and dispatches through the itable with no cross-boundary optimisation. Inspect -XX:+PrintInlining, or make the receiver type explicit.
L4.explanation: This is the actual content of 'interfaces are slow'. It is a profile property of the call site, and the same code is fast or slow depending on the caller.

L4.prompt_tpl: In C++, what do `final` on a class and an anonymous namespace each contribute to devirtualisation?
L4.answer: `final` tells the compiler no further override can exist, so a call through that static type has exactly one target and binds directly. An anonymous namespace gives internal linkage, so the compiler sees every possible derived class in this translation unit and can prove the same thing without LTO.
L4.explanation: Both are ways of closing the world. Without a closed world, a separately compiled TU could add an override, and the direct call would be wrong.

concepts.t: Undefined behavior as an optimization license
concepts.L1: Signed overflow, strict aliasing, null dereference. The compiler assumes UB doesn't happen and optimizes on that assumption. This is why a null check after a dereference gets deleted.
concepts.L2: The mental model that fixes this: UB is not 'the machine does something weird,' it's 'you have given the optimizer a false premise, and it will derive anything from it.'
concepts.L3: The optimiser reasons with theorems of the form "in any defined execution, P holds". UB gives it premises for free: the standard says a defined execution never overflows a signed int, so x+1 > x is true; never dereferences null, so any pointer already dereferenced is non-null; never accesses an object through an incompatible type, so two pointers of different types cannot alias. From a false premise anything follows, which is why the effect is not localised to the offending statement. The compiler propagates the fact backwards along dominance edges, so code that executes strictly before the UB - a bounds check, a null check, a log line - can be deleted as unreachable.

L4.prompt_tpl: `int f(int x) {{ return x*{k} / {k}; }}` at -O2. What does gcc emit, and would the answer change if the parameter were `unsigned`?
L4.answer: It emits `return x;` - signed overflow is UB, so the compiler may assume x*k does not overflow and cancel the division. With unsigned, wraparound is defined, so the cancellation is invalid and the compiler must keep the multiply and divide (it may still strength-reduce them).
L4.explanation: The identity holds mathematically but not in modulo arithmetic; UB is exactly what licenses treating machine ints as mathematical ones.

L4.prompt_tpl: 'UB means the value is unpredictable.' Correct the statement and give the consequence that the wrong version fails to predict.
L4.answer: UB means the entire execution has no defined semantics, not that one expression yields a garbage value. The consequence the wrong model misses is time travel: the compiler can delete code that runs before the UB, so a check you wrote earlier vanishes and the program misbehaves before reaching the offending line.
L4.explanation: Also: UB may be exploited at compile time to delete a whole function body, emit ud2, or fall through into the next function's code.

$ ./app_instr < representative_workload
$ llvm-profdata merge -output=app.profdata default_*.profraw
$ clang -fprofile-use=app.profdata -O2 app.c -o app

# sample-based (no instrumented build, production-safe):
$ perf record -b -e cycles:u -- ./app        # -b: LBR for branch data
$ create_llvm_prof --binary=app --out=app.prof

concepts.L1: Feeding real execution profiles back to the compiler improves branch layout, inlining decisions, and code placement for I-cache locality. Typically 10-20% on large binaries.
concepts.L2: The largest win is usually I-cache, not branch prediction. On server workloads with huge binaries, front-end stalls dominate, and layout matters more than any individual optimization.
concepts.L3: With a profile the compiler knows which branch of each conditional is taken and which call sites are hot. It uses that to lay hot basic blocks contiguously and push cold ones (error paths, logging) into a separate section, so a hot function occupies fewer 64-byte I-cache lines and fewer 4KB iTLB pages; to raise inline thresholds where they pay and lower them where they do not; and to devirtualise indirect calls speculatively. On a multi-hundred-megabyte server binary, front-end stalls from I-cache and iTLB misses commonly account for 15-30% of cycles, which is why layout dominates. Google's AutoFDO and Meta's BOLT report double-digit gains after -O3 has already run.

L4.prompt_tpl: A server binary spends {p}% of cycles stalled in the front end (I-cache and iTLB misses). PGO halves those stalls and changes nothing else. What is the speedup?
L4.answer: For p=20: cycles go from 100 to 90, a 1.11x speedup (about 10%). For p=30: 100 to 85, 1.18x (about 15%). Speedup = 1 / (1 - p/200).
L4.explanation: Straight Amdahl. This is why reported PGO wins cluster at 10-20% on large binaries and near zero on small hot loops that already fit in L1i.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is the biggest PGO win usually instruction cache locality rather than branch prediction, on a {size}MB server binary?
L4.answer: Modern predictors already achieve very high accuracy on the branches that matter, so there is little left to win there. What hardware cannot fix is code layout: a 32KB L1i cannot hold a hot path scattered across hundreds of megabytes, and the iTLB is smaller still. Only the compiler/linker can move the blocks together.
L4.explanation: Hence BOLT, which does the layout as a post-link binary rewrite and gets wins on top of a PGO build that has already run.

# HotSpot tiers: 0 interpreter, 1-3 C1 (fast, profiling), 4 C2 (slow, optimal)
$ java -XX:+PrintCompilation -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining App
$ java -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 App     # C1 only: fast warmup, lower peak

# AOT alternatives
$ native-image App                     # GraalVM: no warmup, no deopt, no profile
$ java -XX:AOTMode=record ... -XX:AOTMode=create   # JDK 24+ AOT cache (Project Leyden)

concepts.L1: JIT sees actual types and actual branch behavior, so it can specialize in ways AOT cannot. AOT has unbounded compile time, no warmup, and predictable latency. Tiered compilation tries to get both.
concepts.L2: Deoptimization is the piece people miss: a JIT speculates, and when the speculation is invalidated it must reconstruct an interpreter frame from optimized state. That machinery is why JIT compilers are so much harder than AOT compilers.
concepts.L3: Deoptimisation is the machinery that makes speculation safe. Compiled code carries a side table mapping each safepoint to the abstract interpreter state - which virtual local lives in which register or spill slot, which objects were scalar-replaced and must be rematerialised on the heap. When an uncommon trap fires (a new receiver type, a null that was never seen, a class loaded that invalidates a CHA assumption), the runtime reconstructs one or more interpreter frames from that table and resumes in the interpreter. This is why a JIT can be aggressive where AOT must be conservative, and why it is far harder to build: every optimisation must preserve enough information to be undone.

L4.prompt_tpl: A {t}-second batch job and a latency-sensitive request service both run the same JVM code. Which benefits more from AOT/native-image, and which from C2, and why?
L4.answer: The short batch job benefits from AOT: it may finish before C2 has compiled anything, so it pays interpretation and compilation cost for no peak-throughput return. The long-lived service benefits from C2, because after warmup its profile-driven speculation beats any static compilation - but it should be measured after warmup, and its p99 will still show deopt and compilation jitter.
L4.explanation: The crossover is roughly where total run time exceeds the time to reach steady state, typically seconds to tens of seconds depending on code footprint.

L4.prompt_tpl: Name a concrete optimisation a JIT can perform that an AOT compiler cannot, and say what mechanism keeps it correct.
L4.answer: Class-hierarchy-based devirtualisation and inlining of a method that only one loaded class implements, or eliminating a null check that has never been observed to fail. Correctness comes from deoptimisation: the runtime records the assumption, and if a later class load or a null arrival invalidates it, the compiled code is discarded and execution falls back to the interpreter.
L4.explanation: An AOT compiler cannot make either assumption because the world is open - a class could be loaded later, and it has no profile saying the null never occurs.

L0.body:
$ gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel -fverbose-asm f.c -o -    # local equivalent of Godbolt
$ objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn -M intel ./a.out | less
$ gcc -O2 -fopt-info-vec-missed f.c               # why a loop did NOT vectorise
$ perf annotate -s hot_function                   # assembly with sampled cycles per line

// In a benchmark, keep the compiler honest:
static void sink(int x) { asm volatile("" :: "r"(x) : "memory"); }   // do not fold this away

concepts.L1: Compiler Explorer, objdump and perf annotate turn 'the compiler probably optimises that' into an observation. Reading a dozen instructions answers whether a call was inlined, a loop vectorised, an allocation elided, or a fence emitted.
concepts.L2: The mistake is reading -O0 output, which faithfully shows the source and tells you nothing about the shipped binary. The second mistake is benchmarking code with an unused result: the optimiser deletes it and you measure an empty loop, which is where most 'this abstraction is free' claims come from.
concepts.L3: Assembly is the only ground truth about what the optimiser decided, because every higher-level claim - inlining, escape analysis, devirtualisation, atomic ordering - has a visible signature there. An inlined call has no call instruction at the site; a vectorised loop uses xmm/ymm/zmm registers and processes several elements per iteration; a heap allocation that was scalar-replaced has no call to operator new; a seq_cst store on x86 is an xchg or a mov followed by mfence; register pressure shows up as mov to and from [rsp+N] inside the loop body. Godbolt makes the loop from source edit to instruction diff a few seconds long, which is what turns it from an occasional exercise into a habit.

L4.prompt_tpl: A microbenchmark loops {n} times calling `expensive(i)` and discards the result. It reports 0.3 ns per call. What happened, and what is the minimal fix?
L4.answer: The call was pure and its result unused, so DCE deleted the body and probably the whole loop; 0.3 ns per iteration is an empty decrement-and-branch or nothing at all. Fix by consuming the result - accumulate into a volatile, pass it to an empty asm volatile sink, or use benchmark::DoNotOptimize.
L4.explanation: Check by reading the assembly of the benchmark loop: if you cannot find the work, it is not there. This single failure invalidates a large fraction of published microbenchmarks.

L4.prompt_tpl: You suspect a small function is not being inlined at -O2. Give two ways to confirm it from the binary and one from the compiler.
L4.answer: From the binary: disassemble the caller and look for a `call` to the callee's symbol, or check whether the callee's symbol still exists with nm. From the compiler: -Winline / -fopt-info-inline (gcc) or -Rpass-missed=inline (clang), which reports each site and the reason.
L4.explanation: Confirming rather than assuming is the whole discipline. The reason given - usually a size budget or an indirect call - also tells you which change would fix it.

$ java -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags App     # JDK 9+ unified logging
$ java -XX:+UseSerialGC -Xmn512m -Xmx4g App                  # explicit young gen size

# Read the log for these, in order of usefulness:
#   allocation rate (MB/s)  = eden size / interval between young GCs
#   promotion rate (MB/s)   = survivors copied out per young GC
#   pause time distribution, not the mean

concepts.L1: Most objects die young. Therefore collect the young generation frequently and cheaply with copying collection, and promote survivors. Copying cost is proportional to live data, not heap size, so a mostly-dead nursery is nearly free to collect.
concepts.L2: The corollary people miss: allocation rate is the tuning knob, not heap size. Reducing allocation reduces GC frequency linearly; growing the heap only delays.
concepts.L3: A copying collector traces from roots, copies each reachable object into a to-space, and then declares the entire from-space free in O(1). Nothing touches the garbage, so cost is proportional to survivors. If 98% of a 512MB eden is dead, a young collection copies 10MB regardless of how large the heap is. Halving allocation rate halves the number of collections and so halves total young GC time; doubling heap size only lengthens the interval between collections while leaving each one's cost roughly unchanged - and it raises the chance that objects which would have died young survive to be promoted, which makes old-gen work worse. That asymmetry is why "just give it more heap" plateaus.

L4.prompt_tpl: A service allocates {rate} MB/s with a {eden} MB eden, of which {surv}% survives each young GC. How often does a young GC run, and how much is copied per collection? Answer with the interval between young GCs in seconds.
L4.answer: Interval = eden / rate seconds. For 1000 MB/s and 512 MB eden: one young GC every 0.512 s. Copied per GC = eden * surv/100; at 5% that is 25.6 MB. Halving the allocation rate halves the GC frequency and so halves total young-GC CPU.
L4.explanation: Do this arithmetic from the GC log rather than guessing: eden size and interval give allocation rate directly, and it is the number that actually predicts GC cost.

L4.prompt_tpl: Young GC pauses are {ms} ms and too frequent. Team A proposes doubling -Xmx. Team B proposes removing a per-request allocation of {n} temporary objects. Who is right and why?
L4.answer: Team B: fewer allocations cut young-GC frequency directly, while a bigger -Xmx does not shrink eden-survivor volume
L4.explanation: Growing the heap delays; reducing allocation removes. The only case for more heap is when the live set genuinely does not fit.
options: Team B: fewer allocations cut young-GC frequency directly, while a bigger -Xmx does not shrink eden-survivor volume
Team A: a larger heap means the collector runs less often, which is exactly the stated problem
Neither: young pause time is set by the size of the live set, so only object lifetime matters

prereqs: RAII: constructors, destructors, and scope

concepts.L1: Generational collection needs to know about old-to-young references. A write barrier records them, typically into a card table marking dirty regions. This is a per-pointer-write cost imposed on all mutator code.
concepts.L2: There is no free generational GC. The barrier cost is paid on every reference store in the entire program, and it's why some low-allocation workloads are faster with a non-generational collector.
concepts.L3: To collect the young generation alone, the collector needs all roots into it, including fields of old objects. Scanning the old generation would cost O(old heap) and defeat the point, so the mutator pays instead: each reference store also marks the card containing the target object, and the young collection scans only dirty cards. Unconditional card marking is 2-3 instructions and one store to a byte the store may share with other threads, so it is cheap but not free. G1's barrier is considerably heavier - a cross-region filter, an SATB pre-barrier load, and an enqueue to a per-thread buffer - which is the main reason G1 gives up throughput relative to Parallel GC.

L4.prompt_tpl: A loop performs {n} reference stores per second. Card marking adds ~3 instructions plus one store per reference write; assume ~1 ns of added cost per barrier. What throughput does the barrier cost, and when would a non-generational collector win?
L4.answer: At 1e8 stores/s: ~0.1 s of CPU per second per core, ~10% overhead. At 1e9: the barrier alone is ~1 s/s, i.e. it dominates. A non-generational or barrier-free collector (Epsilon for short-lived jobs, or a design like Parallel GC's cheaper barrier) wins when the program stores references constantly but allocates little, so it pays the barrier without benefiting from cheap young collections.
L4.explanation: Reference-store-heavy, allocation-light workloads are the case where generational collection is a net loss. Pointer-free primitive arrays pay no barrier at all - one concrete reason primitive collections beat boxed ones.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does storing a primitive int into a field cost no write barrier, while storing a reference does?
L4.answer: The barrier exists only to track pointers into the collected region. An int cannot be a root, so it can never make a young object reachable and needs no record. Only reference stores can create the old-to-young edges the collector must find.
L4.explanation: This is a concrete argument for primitive-specialised collections and for value types (Valhalla): fewer reference fields means fewer barriers and less remembered-set traffic.

prereqs: The generational hypothesis

concepts.t: Tri-color marking and the concurrent problem
concepts.L1: White (unreachable), grey (reached, children unscanned), black (scanned). Concurrent collection breaks if the mutator creates a black→white reference while deleting the only grey→white path. Solved by SATB or incremental-update barriers.
concepts.L2: Being able to state the tri-color invariant and why it's violated is a genuinely differentiating answer. Most engineers know 'GC has phases' and stop there.
concepts.L3: Marking terminates when the grey set is empty, at which point everything white is unreachable and freed. Concurrency threatens this because the mutator can move a reference from a grey object to a black one: the black object is never rescanned, and the grey path is gone, so a live object is collected. A deletion barrier (Yuasa/SATB) shades the overwritten value, preserving the object graph as it stood at mark start; anything dead after that point is collected next cycle, called floating garbage. An insertion barrier (Dijkstra) shades the newly stored pointer, keeping the invariant directly. G1 and Shenandoah use SATB; Go uses a hybrid so stacks stay black without rescanning.

L4.prompt_tpl: During concurrent marking, a mutator executes `black.f = white; grey.f = null;` with no barrier. Trace the colours and say what goes wrong.
L4.answer: After the two stores, the white object is reachable only from a black object. Black is never rescanned, so nothing shades it grey; when marking ends it is still white and is reclaimed while live - a use-after-free. A deletion barrier would have shaded the white object when grey.f was overwritten; an insertion barrier would have shaded it at the store into black.f.
L4.explanation: Both conditions are needed for the bug: a black-to-white edge created AND the last grey-to-white path destroyed. That conjunction is what the two barrier families each break.

L4.prompt_tpl: SATB retains objects that died after marking began. Name that phenomenon and say why the design accepts it.
L4.answer: floating garbage
L4.explanation: SATB marks a snapshot of the heap as it was when the cycle began, so anything that dies mid-cycle is retained until the next one. The design accepts that because a snapshot needs no rescanning of already-blackened objects; the cost is one cycle of extra retention, and the price of avoiding it is either a stop-the-world pause or a re-mark.
