concepts.L1: Region-based, incrementally compacting, with a pause-time target. Collects the regions with most garbage first, hence 'garbage first'. Remembered sets per region track incoming references.
concepts.L2: Remembered set maintenance is G1's dominant cost and scales with cross-region reference density. Workloads with dense object graphs across regions do badly, which is not obvious from the tuning documentation.
concepts.L3: Regions make the collection set a choice rather than a fixed generation boundary: G1 estimates the cost of evacuating each candidate region from its live-data volume and remembered-set size, then packs as many high-yield regions as fit the pause target. The price is the remembered sets. Every cross-region reference store must be recorded, so the barrier enqueues dirty cards and refinement threads process them into per-region structures whose size grows with cross-region pointer density. A workload with a dense, widely scattered object graph therefore pays a large hidden cost in refinement CPU and footprint - up to a fifth of the heap in bad cases - and no tuning flag fixes it.

L4.prompt_tpl: An application allocates many {mb} MB byte arrays with -XX:G1HeapRegionSize={rs}m. What happens to them and what pathology should you expect?
L4.answer: Any object larger than half a region is humongous, so these are allocated directly into a run of contiguous old regions rather than eden. Expect fragmentation and premature full GCs: contiguous runs become hard to find, and older JVMs only reclaimed humongous regions at a full collection. Raising G1HeapRegionSize so the arrays fall under half a region is the usual fix.
L4.explanation: This is one of the most common real G1 incidents and it is invisible unless you read gc+humongous logs.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does G1 lose throughput to Parallel GC even when pauses are acceptable?
L4.answer: Its write barrier is much heavier (cross-region filtering, an SATB pre-barrier load, and enqueueing dirty cards), and concurrent refinement threads consume CPU that Parallel GC does not spend at all. G1 trades total throughput for bounded pause time, which is a bad trade for a batch job.
L4.explanation: Typical figure is 10-20% throughput loss versus Parallel GC. For offline batch work, -XX:+UseParallelGC remains the right choice.

prereqs: Tri-color marking and the concurrent problem
Write barriers and card tables

concepts.L1: Sub-millisecond pauses independent of heap size, via concurrent relocation. ZGC uses colored pointers and load barriers; Shenandoah uses Brooks forwarding pointers.
concepts.L2: The tradeoff is throughput — barrier cost on every load, and higher memory overhead. Low pause is bought with mutator overhead, and for batch workloads that's a bad trade.
concepts.L3: Pause time in a stop-the-world collector scales with the work done in the pause - marking and, worse, relocating live data. These collectors move both phases into the mutator's execution. Because objects move while threads are running, every load of a reference must be validated: ZGC tests colour bits in the pointer and, on a mismatch, fixes up the reference in place before the program sees it; Shenandoah reads through a forwarding word. Pauses then contain only root scanning and handshakes, which is bounded by thread count rather than heap size - sub-millisecond on terabyte heaps. The bill is a barrier on the hottest operation in the language and 5-15% extra footprint.

L4.prompt_tpl: A nightly batch job processing {gb} GB has no latency requirement. Someone switches it to ZGC because 'ZGC is the modern collector'. Predict the outcome.
L4.answer: Throughput drops, typically 10-15%, and the job takes longer: load barriers and concurrent GC CPU buy pause time nobody asked for
L4.explanation: Low pause is purchased with mutator overhead: every reference load runs a load barrier and the concurrent collector competes for CPU with the application. 'Modern' is not a workload characteristic - with no pause-time requirement, Parallel GC finishes the job sooner.

Throughput improves: concurrent relocation means the application never stops, so former pause time becomes useful work
No measurable change: at this heap size collector choice is dominated by allocation rate, which did not change

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is ZGC's pause time independent of heap size when G1's is not?
L4.answer: G1 evacuates its collection set inside the pause, so pause duration scales with the live data in the chosen regions - and the pause target is met by shrinking the collection set, which can fall behind. ZGC relocates concurrently and its pauses contain only root scanning and handshakes, whose cost scales with the number of threads and roots rather than the heap.
L4.explanation: This is why a ZGC pause on a 2 TB heap can be under a millisecond, and why its failure mode is different: allocation stalls when the collector cannot keep up, rather than a long pause.

concepts.L1: Refcounting reclaims promptly and has no pause, but can't collect cycles, and the count updates are expensive under contention. Tracing handles cycles and amortizes cost but pauses.
concepts.L2: They're duals — Bacon, Cheng and Rajan showed every high-performance collector is a hybrid of the two. Swift's ARC plus manual weak references is refcounting with the cycle problem pushed to the programmer.
concepts.L3: Bacon, Cheng and Rajan's framing: tracing computes liveness by starting from roots and following edges forwards; reference counting computes deadness by tracking the same edge changes locally, so it is tracing over the dual graph. Every high-performance collector is then a hybrid - deferred refcounting ignores stack references and traces them, cycle collectors trace candidate subgraphs, generational tracing collectors use write barriers that look exactly like count updates. The engineering difference is where cost lands: refcounting spreads it across the mutator as atomic increments on shared objects (a contended cache line per shared pointer copy), tracing batches it into collector time.

L4.prompt_tpl: Python: `a = []; b = []; a.append(b); b.append(a); del a; del b`. Are the lists freed immediately? What frees them, and what if they had `__del__` methods (CPython {ver}+)?
L4.answer: Not immediately: each still has a refcount of 1 from the other, so refcounting cannot reclaim them. The generational cycle collector frees them at its next run (or on gc.collect()). Since PEP 442 in CPython 3.4, objects with __del__ in cycles ARE collected, with finalisers called before the cycle is broken; before 3.4 they went to gc.garbage and leaked.
L4.explanation: A cycle keeps both refcounts at one, so neither list is freed when the names are deleted. This is the concrete cost of refcounting's incompleteness, and why CPython ships a generational cycle collector alongside it - gc.collect() is what actually reclaims the pair.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is a shared_ptr copy in a {n}-thread hot path often slower than a tracing GC's allocation?
L4.answer: Copying a shared_ptr does an atomic increment on the control block, so every thread sharing the object contends for the same cache line - a locked RMW plus coherence traffic per copy, tens to hundreds of cycles under contention. A tracing GC's fast-path allocation is a thread-local bump of a pointer, a few cycles, and the reclamation cost is deferred and amortised.
L4.explanation: Hence the guidance to pass `const shared_ptr&` or a raw pointer/reference when no ownership transfer occurs: the refcount traffic, not the pointer, is the cost.

$ GODEBUG=gctrace=1 ./app
gc 12 @3.041s 0%: 0.018+1.9+0.007 ms clock, 0.14+0.32/1.8/0+0.061 ms cpu, 4->4->2 MB, 5 MB goal
#   ^cycle ^since start  ^STW sweep term + concurrent mark + STW mark term
#   4->4->2 MB = heap at start -> at end -> live;  next cycle triggered near 2*live (GOGC=100)

$ GOGC=200 ./app          # trade memory for fewer cycles
$ GOMEMLIMIT=4GiB ./app   # soft limit; the collector runs harder as you approach it

concepts.L1: Concurrent, non-moving, non-generational, tri-color with a hybrid write barrier. Optimized for latency at the explicit cost of throughput and fragmentation.
concepts.L2: Non-moving means Go cannot compact, so fragmentation is real and unfixable, and it means Go can pass pointers to C cheaply. The design is a coherent set of tradeoffs, not an incomplete GC.
concepts.L3: Not moving objects is the decision every other property follows from. No read barrier is needed and addresses are stable, so a pointer can be handed to C via cgo; and the size-class allocator (a tcmalloc descendant) is the only defence against fragmentation, which is therefore permanent. Not being generational means every cycle traces the whole live heap, so cost scales with live set rather than allocation - which is why Go's answer to GC pressure is fewer live pointer-bearing objects, and why sync.Pool matters more there than in Java. The hybrid barrier lets goroutine stacks be marked black once and never rescanned, which is what removed the old stop-the-world stack rescan.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Go service has a {live} MB live heap and GOGC={gogc}. At what heap size does the next cycle start, and what happens to CPU cost if you double GOGC? Answer with the heap size in MB at which the next cycle starts.
L4.answer: Target heap = live * (1 + GOGC/100). For live=500 MB, GOGC=100: next cycle at ~1000 MB. Doubling GOGC roughly halves the number of cycles per unit of allocation, so GC CPU roughly halves, at the cost of roughly doubling peak heap.
L4.explanation: Because Go is non-generational, each cycle costs O(live), not O(allocated), so GOGC trades memory directly for GC CPU. GOMEMLIMIT is the safer modern knob - it bounds the heap while letting GOGC stay high.

L4.prompt_tpl: Name two capabilities Go gets from a non-moving collector and one cost it can never fix.
L4.answer: Capabilities: pointers can be passed to C code and remain valid (cheap cgo and syscall interop), and no load/read barrier is needed, so pointer loads are plain loads. Cost: no compaction, so heap fragmentation is permanent and RSS can stay high after a spike even when live data has shrunk.
L4.explanation: These are a coherent design, not an unfinished one. The comparison with ZGC is instructive: ZGC pays a load barrier on every reference read to buy compaction.

concepts.L1: Memory is the only resource a tracing GC manages. File descriptors, sockets, locks and native handles need an explicit scope-bound release: RAII in C++ and Rust, try-with-resources in Java, with in Python, defer in Go.
concepts.L2: Finalizers are not a fallback, they are a liability: they run on an unspecified thread at an unspecified time, may never run at all if the process exits, and an object with a finalizer survives one extra GC cycle and can resurrect itself. Java removed finalize() for these reasons, not for style.
concepts.L3: A tracing collector detects unreachability, which is not the same event as "the program is finished with this object", and it detects it only when it happens to run. So the interval between last use and reclamation is unbounded, and for a resource with a small quota - 1024 file descriptors by default - that interval is where you run out. Finalisation makes it worse by requiring an extra queue: the collector must discover unreachability, resurrect the object to run the finaliser on another thread, then prove unreachability again later. Deterministic schemes invert this: ownership is lexical, release happens at a point you can name, and the GC is left responsible only for memory.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Go function opens {n} files in a loop with `defer f.Close()` inside the loop body. What fails, and what is the fix?
L4.answer: Every deferred Close is queued until the enclosing FUNCTION returns, so all n descriptors stay open at once and the process hits its file-descriptor limit. Fix by moving the body into its own function (so the defer fires per iteration) or by calling Close explicitly at the end of each iteration.
L4.explanation: Go's defer is function-scoped by design, so that it can also run during panic unwinding. Block-scoped defer was considered and rejected.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Java class holds a socket and closes it in an overridden finalize(). Give three independent reasons this is wrong.
L4.answer: One: the finaliser runs at an unspecified later time, so sockets accumulate and the process exhausts descriptors under load. Two: it may never run - the JVM makes no guarantee at exit. Three: it costs a whole extra GC cycle per object and runs on a single shared finaliser thread that can back up unboundedly. finalize() is deprecated for removal; the answer is AutoCloseable with try-with-resources, and Cleaner only as a safety net.
L4.explanation: A Cleaner-based safety net is defensible as a leak detector of last resort. As the primary release mechanism it is the same bug with a newer API.

concepts.t: Threads vs green threads vs async
concepts.L1: OS threads: preemptive, ~8KB-2MB stack, kernel scheduling, context switch ~1-2μs. Green threads (goroutines, virtual threads): user-scheduled, growable stacks, cheap. Async/await: state machine transformation, no stack at all.
concepts.L2: The async coloring problem — async functions can only be awaited from async functions — is a language design consequence, not an inherent property of asynchrony. Go and Java's virtual threads avoid it by keeping the stack.
concepts.L3: An OS thread's cost is the kernel's: a scheduler entry, a kernel stack, a context switch that pollutes cache and TLB, and a user stack whose size must be reserved up front because it cannot move. Green threads move scheduling into user space and make the stack movable (Go copies and relocates it, adjusting pointers, which needs full type information), so a switch is a few register saves and creation is an allocation. Async abolishes the stack entirely: the compiler splits the function at each await and lifts every live local into a struct, so a suspended task costs exactly its live variables, often tens of bytes. That is why a million async tasks fit where a million threads do not.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need {n} concurrent connections, each blocked on I/O with about {live} bytes of live state. Estimate memory for OS threads (1 MB stack reserve each) versus async tasks, and state the real limit in each case.
L4.answer: Threads: n * 1 MB of virtual reservation (100 GB at n=1e5 is already implausible), though RSS is only the touched pages - the practical limits are scheduler overhead and the per-thread kernel stack (typically 8-16 KB of real memory each). Async: n * ~live bytes plus per-task bookkeeping, so 1e6 * 500 B is around 500 MB - the real limit is file descriptors and event-loop throughput.
L4.explanation: The honest comparison is kernel memory and switch cost, not the virtual stack reservation, which is why 'threads use 1 MB each' overstates the case while still reaching the right conclusion.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why do Go and Java virtual threads not suffer the function-colouring problem, while Rust and Python async do?
L4.answer: Go and Java keep a real, movable stack per task, so a blocking call can simply park the task and reschedule the carrier thread - no signature change is needed and ordinary blocking code works unmodified. Rust and Python transform async functions into state machines with no stack, so suspension is only expressible at an await inside a function the compiler rewrote, which forces the async marker to propagate up every caller.
L4.explanation: Colouring is a consequence of the stackless implementation strategy, not of asynchrony. Naming that distinction is the differentiating answer.

concepts.L1: Each worker has a local deque, pushes and pops from one end, steals from the other end of a victim's deque. Minimizes contention because the common case touches only local state.
concepts.L2: Stealing from the opposite end is deliberate: it takes the oldest task, which is likely to be the largest subtree, amortizing the steal cost. This is the detail that shows you've read Cilk rather than just used ForkJoinPool.
concepts.L3: The owner's push and pop touch only its own deque's bottom index and need no atomic RMW except in the single-element case where owner and thief may collide - so the common path is a plain load, store and fence, and contention is zero when everyone has work. Stealing is the rare path, and it costs one CAS on the victim's top index. Taking the oldest task exploits the shape of divide-and-conquer recursion: in a fork-join tree the earliest-pushed task is nearest the root, so it represents the largest unexplored subtree. One steal therefore buys a large amount of work, and Blumofe and Leiserson's bound follows - expected O(T1/P + T-infinity) time with O(P * T-infinity) steal attempts.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why steal from the opposite end of the victim's deque rather than the same end? Give the algorithmic reason, not just 'to avoid contention'.
L4.answer: Two reasons and only one is contention. The oldest task at the far end sits nearest the root of the fork tree, so it carries the largest remaining subtree and one expensive steal amortises over a lot of work. Stealing the newest task would take a leaf, forcing repeated steals. The end separation also means owner and thief touch different cache lines except in the near-empty case.
L4.explanation: Locality is the second-order effect: the owner's newest tasks are the ones whose data is still hot in its cache, so leaving them with the owner is right on both counts.

L4.prompt_tpl: A ForkJoinPool with {p} workers shows near-100% CPU and low throughput on a task that does blocking I/O in each subtask. Diagnose.
L4.answer: Work stealing assumes tasks are CPU-bound and short. Blocking I/O parks the carrier thread with its deque still full, so the pool loses parallelism while idle thieves spin looking for work. The fix is ManagedBlocker, a separate pool for blocking work, or virtual threads - not a larger pool.
L4.explanation: The high CPU is steal-attempt spinning, not useful work. This is the standard failure of running blocking work on the common ForkJoinPool, which is also what parallel streams use.

// Go, CSP: the channel is the first-class thing; the goroutine has no name.
ch := make(chan int)        // unbuffered: send blocks until a receiver is ready
ch <- 1                     // rendezvous
v, ok := <-ch               // ok == false once closed and drained

% Erlang, actors: the process id is first-class; the mailbox is unbounded.
Pid = spawn(fun loop/0),
Pid ! {work, 1},            % asynchronous, never blocks
receive {work, N} -> ... end.

concepts.L1: CSP (Go): channels are first-class, processes anonymous, synchronous rendezvous by default. Actors (Erlang, Akka): addresses are first-class, mailboxes unbounded and asynchronous.
concepts.L2: The consequential difference is backpressure. CSP's unbuffered channels give it for free; actor mailboxes are unbounded by default and that's how actor systems OOM.
concepts.L3: An unbuffered channel send cannot complete until a receiver takes the value, so a slow consumer directly stalls its producer - backpressure is the default and requires no design. An actor send appends to a mailbox and returns, so a slow consumer's queue grows without bound; the producer learns nothing and memory absorbs the mismatch until the node dies. Erlang's answer is supervision plus protocol-level flow control; Akka added bounded mailboxes and Reactive Streams demand signalling to retrofit it. The tradeoff is real in the other direction too: rendezvous couples the two parties' liveness, which is why Go deadlocks are easy to write and actor systems are easier to make fault-isolated.

L4.prompt_tpl: Go: `ch := make(chan int)` then in main `ch <- {v}` with no other goroutine. What happens, and what changes with `make(chan int, {n})`?
L4.answer: Deadlock: the runtime detects that all goroutines are asleep and panics with 'fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!'. With a buffer of n, the first n sends complete immediately and the (n+1)th blocks, giving the same deadlock later.
L4.explanation: The unbuffered send is a rendezvous, so it needs a ready receiver, not just a place to put the value. Buffering delays the coupling; it does not remove it.

L4.prompt_tpl: An actor system OOMs under a {x}x traffic spike while a channel-based service merely slows down. Explain the structural reason.
L4.answer: Unbounded mailboxes turn a rate mismatch into memory growth: producers keep accepting work at full speed because sending never blocks, and the queue absorbs the difference until the heap is exhausted. A bounded or unbuffered channel converts the same mismatch into blocked producers, which propagates the slowdown to the source - the load shedding happens at the edge instead of in the heap.
L4.explanation: This is why bounded queues everywhere is a standing rule in production systems, and why Akka Streams and Reactive Streams exist as a layer over raw actors.

prereqs: Threads vs green threads vs async

concepts.L1: Task lifetimes nest with lexical scope; a scope doesn't exit until its children complete. Makes cancellation and error propagation composable rather than ad hoc.
concepts.L2: The insight is that unstructured task spawning is the goto of concurrency — it breaks the invariant that control flow follows program structure, and everything that follows from that (leaked tasks, orphaned errors) is the same class of problem.
concepts.L3: Structured programming won by guaranteeing single-entry, single-exit blocks, which makes local reasoning and stack-based resource management possible. A bare spawn breaks exactly that: the child outlives the syntactic construct that created it, so there is no scope whose exit can join it, no frame that owns its errors, and no natural place to deliver cancellation. Every downstream problem - leaked tasks, exceptions swallowed in a detached future, cancellation implemented as an ad hoc flag, a timeout that returns while the work continues - is the same failure. Nesting lifetimes restores the invariant: the scope is the owner, join is the exit, and a child's failure has an obvious place to go.

L4.prompt_tpl: `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(this::fetch).orTimeout({s}, SECONDS)` returns on timeout and the caller retries. After a load spike the service has {n} in-flight fetches and dies. Explain.
L4.answer: orTimeout completes the returned future exceptionally but does not cancel or interrupt the underlying task, which keeps running and holding its connection and buffers. Each retry adds another. The timeout gave the caller an answer without giving the work an owner - the unstructured-spawn failure exactly.
L4.explanation: Under a structured scope the timeout is scope-level and its exit cancels the children, so a timed-out request stops consuming resources.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is 'unstructured task spawning is the goto of concurrency' more than an analogy?
L4.answer: Both break the same invariant: that control flow follows program structure, so a block's exit implies completion of everything it started. Once that fails, the mechanisms that depend on it - stack-based resource release, exception propagation to a caller, timeouts, cancellation - all stop composing and must each be rebuilt by hand.
L4.explanation: Dijkstra's argument against goto was about the difficulty of reasoning, not about jumps per se. The same argument transfers exactly.

concepts.L1: The hard part isn't the algorithm, it's knowing when it's safe to free. Hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, RCU, or deferred reclamation via a GC.
concepts.L2: This is why lock-free data structures are much easier in GC'd languages. In C++ the reclamation scheme is usually more complex than the algorithm, and 'we wrote it lock-free' without naming a reclamation scheme is a red flag.
concepts.L3: A lock-free reader loads a pointer then dereferences it; between those instructions another thread may unlink and free the node, so the read is a use-after-free, and no atomics on the pointer fix it: the hazard is the object's lifetime, not the pointer's value. Every scheme proves no reader holds the object: hazard pointers make readers publish their references so a retiring thread can scan and defer, at a store-load fence per read; epoch schemes and RCU free only what was retired two epochs ago, cheaper per read but with unbounded deferral if a reader stalls. A tracing GC solves it as a side effect, which is why the same queue is a page of code in Java and several in C++.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C++ lock-free stack does `Node* old = head.load(); while (!head.compare_exchange_weak(old, old->next)) {{}} return old;` with {n} concurrent poppers. Name both bugs.
L4.answer: First, use-after-free: another thread can pop and delete the node between the load and the read of old->next, so the CAS argument dereferences freed memory. Second, ABA: the node can be freed, a new node allocated at the same address and pushed, and the CAS then succeeds against a stale next pointer, corrupting the stack. Both are fixed by a reclamation scheme - hazard pointers or epochs - not by changing the memory ordering.
L4.explanation: This is the canonical demonstration that reclamation, not the CAS, is the hard part. Note both bugs have the same root cause: memory reuse.

L4.prompt_tpl: Compare hazard pointers and epoch-based reclamation on read cost and worst-case memory. Which would you pick for a read-mostly index with occasional long readers?
L4.answer: Hazard pointers cost a store plus a fence per protected read but bound the deferred memory by (threads * hazards per thread). Epochs cost only an epoch announcement on entering a critical section - much cheaper per read - but a single stalled reader pins every retired object, so memory is unbounded. With occasional long readers, hazard pointers are the safer choice.
L4.explanation: This tradeoff is exactly why the Linux kernel documents RCU grace periods so carefully: a reader that sleeps in a read-side critical section is a memory leak in the making.

concepts.L1: CAS succeeds because the value matches, but it was changed to B and back to A meanwhile. Solved with tagged pointers, double-width CAS, or a reclamation scheme that prevents reuse.
concepts.L2: ABA is fundamentally an aliasing problem caused by memory reuse — which is why epoch-based reclamation solves it as a side effect rather than needing a separate fix.
concepts.L3: CAS asks "does this word still equal the value I read?" and infers "then nothing has changed". The inference is invalid whenever the same value can recur, which for pointers means whenever an address can be freed and reallocated. A monotonic tag makes the compared word encode history rather than state, so recurrence is detectable - at the cost of a wider atomic. A reclamation scheme removes the premise instead: if a node cannot be freed while any thread might CAS against it, the address cannot be reused, and ABA becomes unreachable without any tagging. Load-linked/store-conditional avoids it at the hardware level, since SC fails if the reservation was broken by any intervening write.

L4.prompt_tpl: Lock-free stack with nodes A -> B -> C. Thread 1 reads head=A, next=B, then is preempted. Thread 2 pops A, pops B, pushes A back (reusing the node). Thread 1 resumes and its CAS(head, A -> B) executes. What is the stack afterwards?
L4.answer: The CAS succeeds because head is A again, and head becomes B - but B was already popped and freed. The stack now points at reclaimed memory, and C is lost. A version tag would have made the CAS fail.
L4.explanation: Note the failure needs no data race in the memory-model sense; every access was atomic. The bug is that value equality was taken as proof of no intervening modification.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does epoch-based reclamation eliminate ABA without any explicit ABA fix?
L4.answer: ABA requires the same address to be handed out twice while a thread still holds it. Epoch reclamation guarantees a retired node is not freed until every thread that could have observed it has left its critical section, so the allocator cannot return that address to anyone during the window - the recurrence is impossible rather than merely detected.
L4.explanation: This is the sense in which ABA is an aliasing problem caused by memory reuse rather than an independent flaw in CAS.

L0.body:
# Amdahl:  S(N) = 1 / (s + (1-s)/N)                     -> asymptote at 1/s
# USL:      X(N) = (lambda * N) / (1 + a*(N-1) + b*N*(N-1))
#           a = contention (serialisation, queueing), b = coherency (crosstalk)
# b > 0 gives a maximum, then decline:  N_max = sqrt((1 - a) / b)

import numpy as np
N = np.arange(1, 65); a, b, lam = 0.03, 0.0005, 1.0
X = lam*N / (1 + a*(N-1) + b*N*(N-1))
print(N[X.argmax()], X.max())     # the knee, and throughput at it

concepts.L1: Amdahl caps speedup by the serial fraction. USL adds a coherency term that makes throughput decrease past a point, which matches real systems where Amdahl doesn't.
concepts.L2: USL is the more useful law and almost nobody cites it. The coherency penalty term is why adding threads past the knee makes things actively worse rather than merely plateauing.
concepts.L3: Amdahl models one cost: work that must run serially, which bounds speedup but never makes more workers actively harmful. Real systems get worse past a point because workers must agree - cache lines bounce between cores, a lock's waiters must be woken and handed off, replicas exchange state - and that cost grows with the number of pairs, hence the N(N-1) term. Gunther's USL is exactly a two-parameter queueing model: alpha is serialisation you could in principle remove by sharding, beta is pairwise crosstalk you can only remove by not sharing. Fit it to three or four measured load points and it predicts the knee, which is far more actionable than an unbounded scaling assumption.

L4.prompt_tpl: A system fits USL with alpha={a} and beta={b}. Where is peak throughput, and what does adding workers beyond it do? Answer with the worker count at peak throughput.
L4.answer: N_peak = sqrt((1 - alpha)/beta). For alpha=0.05, beta=0.001: sqrt(0.995/0.001) = ~31.5, so about 31 workers. Beyond it throughput falls, because the coherency term grows quadratically while the added capacity grows linearly - adding workers reduces total work done.
L4.explanation: This is the shape everyone has seen in production and few can name: a throughput curve that peaks and then declines under increasing concurrency.

L4.prompt_tpl: Throughput rises to {n} threads then falls. Amdahl says it should plateau. What does USL attribute the decline to, and what would you change in the code?
L4.answer: The coherency term: pairwise coordination cost, typically a shared cache line (a hot counter, a shared lock word, false sharing) whose ownership bounces between cores, or lock handoff/wakeup traffic. The fix is to remove sharing - per-thread or per-core counters aggregated on read, sharded locks, padded structures - rather than to reduce the serial section.
L4.explanation: Alpha and beta call for different remedies: alpha is fixed by sharding the serial section, beta only by eliminating shared state. Conflating them leads to tuning that does nothing.

concepts.L1: Lifetimes as region inference. Variance in lifetime parameters. Pin and self-referential structs. Send/Sync as auto-traits and what unsafe impl actually asserts. Interior mutability as the escape hatch that keeps the model sound.
concepts.L2: Send/Sync is the piece that makes Rust's concurrency claim work, and most Rust users can't state what they mean. Send = safe to move across threads. Sync = &T is Send. Rc is neither; Arc is both.
concepts.L3: Send and Sync are auto traits: the compiler derives them structurally, so a struct is Send if all its fields are. That derivation is what makes `thread::spawn` require F: Send and so reject sharing an Rc across threads: Rc's refcount is a plain integer, and the type system stops the race with no special-case rule anywhere. Arc uses atomic counts and is therefore Send and Sync. `unsafe impl Send` is you asserting the property the compiler could not derive, and the obligation is real: every cross-thread use must be sound. Lifetimes are the second half: region inference on MIR, erased before codegen, so they cost nothing and can never be inspected.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does `Rc<RefCell<Vec<{T}>>>` fail to compile when moved into `thread::spawn`, and which single change makes it work?
L4.answer: Rc is neither Send nor Sync because its reference count is non-atomic, so spawn's F: Send bound is not satisfied. Replace Rc with Arc and RefCell with Mutex (or RwLock): Arc gives atomic counts, and RefCell is Send but not Sync, so it cannot be shared behind an Arc.
L4.explanation: Two independent problems, and people usually fix only the Rc half. RefCell's dynamic borrow flag is also non-atomic, which is exactly why it is not Sync.

L4.prompt_tpl: What does `unsafe impl Send for T` actually assert, and what does it NOT do?
L4.answer: It asserts to the compiler that moving a T to another thread is sound - typically that any raw pointers it owns are uniquely owned and that no non-atomic shared state is reachable through it. It does not add any synchronisation, generate any code, or get checked; it is a promise, and if it is wrong the resulting UB is entirely yours.
L4.explanation: This is the general shape of unsafe in Rust: it never turns off checks on the code inside, it lets you assert obligations the checker cannot verify.

concepts.L1: Value categories (lvalue, prvalue, xvalue), move semantics and when moves are elided, RAII, the rule of zero/three/five, template instantiation and SFINAE, then concepts. Strict aliasing.
concepts.L2: Return value optimization is mandatory since C++17 for prvalues, which changes the correct idiom — returning by value is now strictly better than out-parameters, and a lot of codebases still carry the old wisdom.
concepts.L3: In C++17 a prvalue is no longer an object that gets copied; it is an initialiser, and the object is constructed directly in the caller's storage. `return std::string("x")` therefore involves no constructor call beyond the one you wrote, no move, and no reliance on optimiser goodwill - it is required, and works even for non-movable types. The old out-parameter idiom (`void get(std::string& out)`) now costs strictly more: the caller must default-construct the object first and the function assigns into it. Named locals are weaker: NRVO is an optimisation, not a guarantee, though every compiler does it - so `return std::move(local)` pessimises by suppressing it.

L4.prompt_tpl: How many string constructor calls occur in `std::string f() {{ return std::string({n}, 'x'); }} auto s = f();` under C++17? What about `std::string g() {{ std::string t({n}, 'x'); return std::move(t); }}`?
L4.answer: f: exactly one - guaranteed copy elision constructs the string directly in s's storage. g: two - one for t, then a move construction, because std::move turns the return operand into an xvalue and disables NRVO. Writing std::move on a return of a local is a pessimisation.
L4.explanation: This is the concrete reason 'return by value' beats out-parameters in modern C++, and why the reflex `return std::move(x)` is wrong.

L4.prompt_tpl: `std::string a = "{w}"; std::string b = std::move(a); std::cout << a.size();` The author expects 0. Is that guaranteed?
L4.answer: No: a moved-from standard library object is valid but unspecified, so size() may be 0 or anything else
L4.explanation: Valid-but-unspecified means you may only call operations with no preconditions: destroy, assign, or query in a way you do not depend on. Do not test for emptiness after a move.

>>> import dis, sys
>>> dis.dis(compile("x += 1", "<s>", "exec"))
  LOAD_NAME  x / LOAD_CONST 1 / BINARY_OP += / STORE_NAME x   # four bytecodes, not one

>>> sys.getrefcount([])            # refcount plus the temporary argument reference
>>> import gc; gc.collect()        # the CYCLE collector, generational, three generations

$ python3.13t -c "import sys; print(sys._is_gil_enabled())"   # free-threaded build

concepts.L1: Reference counting plus a cycle collector. The GIL, what it does and doesn't protect. CPython's bytecode and frame objects. The 3.11+ specializing adaptive interpreter. Free-threaded builds in 3.13+.
concepts.L2: The GIL protects interpreter internals, not your data structures. `list.append` is atomic because it's one bytecode; `x += 1` is not. People conflate 'GIL exists' with 'my Python code is thread-safe.'
concepts.L3: The interpreter releases the GIL between bytecode instructions (default 5 ms), so any bytecode sequence can be interrupted at an instruction boundary. `x += 1` on a shared integer compiles to load, add, store - a thread can be switched out between the add and the store, so increments are lost as in any other language. `lst.append(v)` reaches C code that runs to completion inside one bytecode with the GIL held, which is why it happens to be atomic - an implementation accident the free-threaded build now upholds with per-object locks. Specialisation (PEP 659) then rewrites hot bytecodes in place with guarded type-specialised variants, which is what gives 3.11+ its speedup without a JIT.

L4.prompt_tpl: {t} threads each execute `for _ in range({n}): counter += 1` on a shared module-level int in CPython 3.12. What is the final value?
L4.answer: Less than t*n, and non-deterministic. The increment is four bytecodes and the GIL can be released between them, so updates are lost. The GIL prevents interpreter corruption, not lost updates. Use itertools.count with a lock, or threading.Lock around the increment.
L4.explanation: For small n it may happen to come out right because a thread finishes within one GIL slice - which is what makes this bug so persistent.

L4.prompt_tpl: Under the GIL, does `list.append` need a lock? Does `d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + {n}`?
L4.answer: append does not, in CPython: it is a single bytecode reaching C that runs with the GIL held. The dict update does: it is a get, an add and a store as separate operations, so two threads can both read the old value. The first answer is a CPython implementation detail, not a language guarantee.
L4.explanation: Rely on it only if you have decided to depend on CPython. Under the free-threaded build the guarantee is preserved by explicit per-object locking, but the composite operation is still a race.

concepts.L1: G-M-P model: goroutines, OS threads, processors. Work stealing across P's, handoff on syscall block, asynchronous preemption via signals since 1.14. Channels as a queue plus a wait list, not magic.
concepts.L2: Before 1.14 a tight loop with no function calls could not be preempted, and would hang the collector. Knowing that history explains why Go's scheduler looks the way it does.
concepts.L3: P exists to bound the number of goroutines running Go code to GOMAXPROCS while allowing many more Ms to exist for blocked syscalls. When a goroutine enters a syscall, the M keeps the thread but releases the P, so another M can pick the P up and keep the CPU busy; on return it tries to reacquire a P, otherwise parking on the global queue. Before 1.14 preemption depended on cooperative checks inserted at function prologues, so a loop with no calls and no allocation never yielded, blocking a stop-the-world GC phase indefinitely. Asynchronous preemption sends SIGURG and the handler parks the goroutine at an async-safe point, which required precise stack maps at far more program points.

L4.prompt_tpl: Go 1.13: `go func() {{ for {{ x++ }} }}()` alongside normal work, GOMAXPROCS={p}. What happens at the next GC, and what changed in 1.14?
L4.answer: The loop contains no function call, allocation or channel operation, so there is no cooperative preemption point. In 1.13 the goroutine cannot be preempted, so the stop-the-world phase waits for it forever and the program hangs. Since 1.14 the runtime sends SIGURG and the signal handler preempts it at an async-safe point.
L4.explanation: With GOMAXPROCS=1 it hangs immediately; with more Ps it hangs at the next GC, when every P must reach a safe point. Knowing this history explains why the runtime carries stack maps for so many PCs.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does a blocking syscall not consume a P, while a CPU-bound goroutine does?
L4.answer: A blocked syscall leaves the OS thread waiting in the kernel and running no Go code, so the runtime detaches the P and hands it to another M, keeping GOMAXPROCS worth of Go execution alive. A CPU-bound goroutine is executing Go code and must hold a P for as long as it runs.
L4.explanation: This is why thousands of goroutines blocked in file I/O do not throttle the program, while GOMAXPROCS CPU-bound goroutines saturate it.

concepts.L1: Bytecode, class loading and the delegation model, invokedynamic and how lambdas actually compile, the JIT tiers, JFR for production profiling.
concepts.L2: Lambdas don't compile to anonymous classes — they compile to invokedynamic with a bootstrap that spins the implementation at first call. That's why lambda-heavy code has different startup and inlining behavior.
concepts.L3: invokedynamic leaves the call target unspecified in the class file and names a bootstrap method instead. The first execution calls it, LambdaMetafactory generates a class implementing the functional interface (a hidden class since JDK 15) that forwards to the synthetic method holding the body, and links it into a bound CallSite; every later execution is a direct call the JIT can inline through. The consequences are practical: no class file per lambda, so jar size stays flat and class loading is deferred to first use, but each distinct lambda pays class spinning at that first call - measurable in startup-sensitive services, which is what Project Leyden's AOT class loading targets.

L4.prompt_tpl: A class defines {n} lambdas. How many .class files does javac emit for them, and where does each body live? Answer with the number of extra .class files javac emits.
L4.answer: Zero extra class files. Each lambda body is compiled into a private static synthetic method (`lambda$main$0` and so on) of the enclosing class, and the implementing class is generated at run time by LambdaMetafactory on first execution. An anonymous inner class, by contrast, would emit `Outer$1.class`.
L4.explanation: Check with javap -p: you will see the synthetic methods and the BootstrapMethods attribute, and no extra files on disk.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does a {n}-lambda-heavy application start more slowly than the equivalent with anonymous classes, despite emitting fewer class files?
L4.answer: Each distinct lambda call site runs its bootstrap on first execution: LambdaMetafactory spins a hidden class, defines it, and links a CallSite. That is more work per site than loading a precompiled class file, and it happens lazily during startup rather than being amortised by the class loader.
L4.explanation: This is precisely what CDS, the AOT cache in JDK 24+ and Leyden's condensers exist to remove: they persist the linked state across runs.

int   *p[10];        /* array of 10 pointers to int          */
int  (*q)[10];       /* pointer to an array of 10 ints       */
int  (*f)(void);     /* pointer to function returning int    */
char *(*g[3])(int);  /* array of 3 pointers to functions taking int, returning char*  */

typedef int (*handler_t)(void*);   /* name the shape once, then use it */
handler_t table[8];

/* The rule: start at the identifier, go RIGHT while you can, then LEFT.
   () and [] bind tighter than *, so parentheses are what change the reading. */

concepts.L1: A C declaration mirrors the expression that yields the base type: `int *p[10]` says `*p[i]` is an int. Read outward from the identifier, right before left, with () and [] binding tighter than *.
concepts.L2: `int* a, b;` declares one pointer and one int - the * belongs to the declarator, not the type, which is why C style puts it against the name. This is also why `typedef char* String; const String s;` makes the POINTER const, not the characters.
concepts.L3: C has no separate type syntax: a declaration is written as the expression that produces a value of the base type, with the identifier where the value would appear. `int *p[10]` therefore asserts that `*p[i]` has type int, and since [] binds tighter than *, p is the array. Adding parentheses in `int (*q)[10]` forces the dereference to happen first, so q is the pointer. The same rule generates function pointer syntax and explains why the declarator, not the type, carries the *. The practical response is to stop parsing them in your head: use a typedef or `using` alias for anything past one level, and check yourself with cdecl.

L4.prompt_tpl: Give the English reading of `void (*signal(int, void (*)(int)))(int);` and then rewrite it with a typedef.
L4.answer: signal is a function taking an int and a pointer-to-function(int)->void, and returning a pointer-to-function(int)->void. With a typedef: `typedef void (*sighandler_t)(int); sighandler_t signal(int, sighandler_t);`
L4.explanation: This is the real declaration from signal.h, and the reason POSIX defines sighandler_t. If your declaration needs a diagram, it needs a typedef.

L4.prompt_tpl: `int* a, b, c;` then `b = &x;` fails to compile with 'assignment to int from int *'. Explain in one sentence.
L4.answer: Only a is a pointer: the * is part of a's declarator, not part of a type shared by the declaration, so b and c are plain ints.
L4.explanation: Declare one variable per line, or write `int *a, *b, *c;`. This is why K&R style attaches the asterisk to the name.

L0.cloze:
/* In almost every expression an array {{c1::decays}} to a pointer to its first element.
   The exceptions: as the operand of {{c2::sizeof}}, of {{c3::&}}, and a string literal
   initialising a char array.
   An array parameter is silently rewritten to a {{c4::pointer}}, so sizeof inside the
   function returns {{c5::8}} on a 64-bit target. */

concepts.L1: An array is not a pointer; it is a block of N objects whose name converts to a pointer to its first element in nearly every expression. The exceptions are sizeof, &, and string-literal initialisation.
concepts.L2: A function can never receive an array. `void f(int a[10])` is rewritten to `int *a`, so the 10 is unchecked documentation and sizeof(a) is the pointer size - which is why every C API that takes an array also takes a length, and why sizeof-based bounds checks silently break when the code moves into a function.
concepts.L3: The type of `arr` is int[10] and the type of `&arr[0]` is int*; the conversion between them is a language rule applied to the expression, not a property of the object. That single rule explains the surprises: sizeof and & are specified to operate on the array type before conversion, so they see 40 bytes and int(*)[10]; `arr + 1` advances by one int because the decayed type is int*, while `&arr + 1` advances by forty bytes because the type is a pointer to the whole array. Subscripting is defined as `*(a + i)`, and since addition commutes, `3[arr]` compiles. Parameter adjustment removes the size from the type entirely, which is why C's memory safety is length arguments all the way down.

L4.prompt_tpl: `int a[{n}]; printf("%td %td", (char*)(a+1) - (char*)a, (char*)(&a+1) - (char*)a);` on x86-64. What prints? Answer with the second printed value.
L4.answer: 4 and 4*n. a decays to int*, so a+1 advances one int (4 bytes). &a has type int(*)[n], so &a+1 advances one whole array, 4n bytes: 20 for n=5, 40 for n=10.
L4.explanation: &arr + 1 is the idiomatic way to get a one-past-the-end pointer for the whole array, and is exactly why the two expressions differ.

L4.prompt_tpl: `void copy(char dst[{n}], const char *src) {{ memcpy(dst, src, sizeof(dst)); }}` Why is this wrong, and what does sizeof return?
L4.answer: dst is a pointer, not an array - the parameter's array type was adjusted away - so sizeof(dst) is 8 and the function copies 8 bytes regardless of n. The size must be passed as a separate argument.
L4.explanation: gcc warns with -Wsizeof-pointer-memaccess. C23's `char dst[static 64]` documents a minimum but still does not make sizeof work.

concepts.L1: Members are laid out in declaration order at offsets satisfying each member's alignment, with padding inserted between and after. The struct's own alignment is the largest member's, and its size is rounded up to a multiple of that.
concepts.L2: Trailing padding exists so that arrays of the struct keep every element aligned - which is why sizeof is 12 rather than 9 in the classic case. It also means memcmp on structs can compare uninitialised padding bytes and report a difference between two structs with identical members.
concepts.L3: Hardware requires (or strongly prefers) that an N-byte scalar sit at an address that is a multiple of N, so the compiler inserts padding to guarantee it, and cannot reorder members because C fixes declaration order as part of the ABI. Sorting fields from widest to narrowest therefore removes most padding mechanically: {char,int,char} costs 12 bytes, {int,char,char} costs 8. At scale this is a cache-density argument, not a memory-cost argument - a 33% smaller struct means a third more elements per 64-byte line. Padding bytes have indeterminate values, which is why struct comparison must be field-by-field and why zeroing with memset before serialising is a real practice.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64: sizeof for `struct S {{ char a; {T} b; char c; }}`, and for the same three members ordered b, a, c?
L4.answer: For int (align 4): 12, then 8. For double (align 8): 24, then 16. For short (align 2): 6, then 6 - short needs only 1 byte of padding after a, and the reordered version pads 1 byte at the end, so both are 6.
L4.explanation: Work it out as: place each member at the next offset divisible by its alignment, then round the total up to the struct alignment. The short case shows that reordering is not always a win.

L4.prompt_tpl: A network struct is declared `__attribute__((packed))` and a pointer to its 4-byte field is passed to a function expecting `uint32_t*` on an {arch} target. What goes wrong?
L4.answer: The packed field may sit at an unaligned address, so taking its address produces a uint32_t* that violates the type's alignment requirement - undefined behaviour, and on targets without unaligned access support the dereference faults or silently reads the wrong bytes. Copy the field with memcpy into a properly aligned local instead.
L4.explanation: On x86 the same code appears to work because unaligned loads are permitted, just slower. This is the classic bug that only appears after porting.

L0.cloze:
/* At file scope, `static` means {{c1::internal linkage}}: the symbol is not exported.
   Inside a function, `static` means {{c2::static storage duration}}: one object for the
   whole program, initialised {{c3::once}}.
   `extern` introduces a {{c4::declaration}}, not a definition.
   Inspect what was actually emitted with `{{c5::nm}} -C obj.o`. */

concepts.L1: Scope decides what names are visible where; linkage decides whether two translation units' names refer to the same object; storage duration decides when the object exists. static touches linkage at file scope and duration inside a block.
concepts.L2: A `static` function-local in C++ has thread-safe initialisation guaranteed since C++11 - the compiler emits a guard variable and an atomic check - which is why the Meyers singleton is correct without a mutex. In C there is no such guarantee, and the initialiser must be a constant expression.
concepts.L3: These are three independent axes that C spells with two overloaded keywords. Internal linkage means the compiler emits a local symbol (nm shows lowercase t or b) that the linker will not match against anything in another object file, which is why two files can each define `static int counter` with no conflict. Static storage duration puts the object in .data or .bss rather than on the stack, so it survives across calls and is zero-initialised before main. Automatic duration is the stack frame. Confusing them produces the two classic errors: a `static` in a header giving every including file its own private copy, and a missing `extern` producing multiple definitions at link time.

L4.prompt_tpl: A header contains `static int cache_size = {n};` and is included by {k} .c files, each of which modifies it. Why does the value never appear to propagate?
L4.answer: static gives internal linkage, so each translation unit gets its own private copy of the object. There are k independent variables with the same name, and a write in one is invisible to the others. The fix is `extern int cache_size;` in the header and a single definition in one .c file.
L4.explanation: It links cleanly, which is what makes it hard - the linker has no conflict to report because no symbol is exported at all. nm on each object file shows a lowercase d or b instead of an uppercase D or B.

L4.prompt_tpl: `void f(void) {{ static int n = 0; int m = 0; n++; m++; printf("%d %d ", n, m); }}` called {k} times. What prints?
L4.answer: For k=3: '1 1 2 1 3 1 '. n has static storage duration so one object persists across calls and its initialiser runs once; m is automatic and is created and initialised anew on each call.
L4.explanation: Note where the initialiser runs: n lives in .data (or .bss if zero) and is initialised at load time, before main, not on the first call. m is a fresh stack slot each call. Both are invisible outside the translation unit, but only one survives between calls.

/* `const char *p` : the {{c1::pointee}} is const.  `char * const p` : the {{c2::pointer}} is const.
   `{{c3::restrict}}` promises no aliasing, letting the compiler keep values in registers
   across stores through other pointers.
   `volatile` forbids the compiler from {{c4::eliding}} or reordering the access. */

concepts.L1: const marks an object or access as read-only for the type checker; volatile marks an access as externally observable; restrict promises the compiler that no other pointer reaches the same object in this scope. Only restrict is a claim the compiler acts on for optimisation.
concepts.L2: const is not a promise the object never changes - it is a promise this access will not change it, and casting it away to modify an object that is genuinely const is UB. It also enables almost no optimisation on pointers, because another non-const pointer may alias the same object. restrict is the keyword that actually pays.
concepts.L3: Without restrict, a function taking two pointers of the same type must assume they may alias, so after a store through one it must reload through the other - the classic reason `void add(float *a, const float *b, int n)` fails to vectorise. restrict is the programmer asserting the negative, and it is worth a factor of several on numeric kernels. Nothing checks it; violating it is UB and the failure is a wrong answer, not a crash, which is exactly the difference between memcpy (restrict, undefined on overlap) and memmove (defined, and slower for it). const carries no such license, because const on a parameter says only that this pointer will not write - another pointer still may.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can `void scale(float *out, const float *in, int n)` not be vectorised as well as the same function with `restrict` on both pointers, even though `in` is const?
L4.answer: const only says this function will not write through `in`. It does not say `in` and `out` point to different objects, so the compiler must assume a store to out[i] may change in[i+1] and must reload after every store, serialising the loop. restrict asserts non-aliasing and unlocks vectorisation.
L4.explanation: Check it on Godbolt: the restrict version uses xmm/ymm registers, the const version does not. Or use -fopt-info-vec-missed, which names aliasing as the reason.

L4.prompt_tpl: `memcpy(buf + {k}, buf, n)` with overlapping ranges works in testing and corrupts data after a compiler upgrade. Explain.
L4.answer: memcpy's parameters are restrict-qualified, so overlapping arguments are undefined behaviour. The old implementation happened to copy forwards byte by byte; the new one copies backwards or in wide SIMD chunks, and the overlap corrupts. memmove is the defined operation for overlapping ranges.
L4.explanation: This is a real class of glibc-upgrade incident. It also demonstrates that UB failures are often triggered by a library or compiler change, not by a code change.

concepts.t: Integer conversions, promotion, and the signedness traps

L0.cloze:
/* Any type narrower than int is {{c1::promoted}} to int before arithmetic.
   When operands have the same rank but different signedness, the result type is
   {{c2::unsigned}} - so comparing a negative int with an unsigned yields a surprise.
   Signed overflow is {{c3::undefined}}; unsigned overflow is defined to {{c4::wrap}}.
   Warning flag: -W{{c5::sign-compare}}. */

concepts.L1: Operands narrower than int are promoted to int, then the usual arithmetic conversions bring both to a common type - which, at equal rank, is the unsigned one. Signed overflow is UB; unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo 2^N.
concepts.L2: `if (len - 1 >= 0)` is always true when len is size_t, because the subtraction wraps to a huge value rather than going negative. Every loop written as `for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)` is infinite for the same reason, and neither is a warning by default.
concepts.L3: The conversions exist because C's arithmetic is defined on int and wider, so a compiler may implement 8- and 16-bit arithmetic using 32-bit registers. Promotion happens first and preserves value where int can represent the whole source range, which is why unsigned char arithmetic happens in signed int and wraps only on store-back. The usual arithmetic conversions then pick a common type, and the rule that at equal rank unsigned wins is what makes mixed comparisons quietly wrong: the signed value is reinterpreted modulo 2^N first. On LP64 the rule bites differently than on 32-bit: int stays 32 bits while size_t grows, so a harmless mixed expression becomes a 64-bit surprise.

L4.prompt_tpl: `size_t n = {n}; for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) sum += a[i];` What happens?
L4.answer: Infinite loop and out-of-bounds access. i is unsigned, so i >= 0 is always true; after i == 0 the decrement wraps to SIZE_MAX and a[i] reads far out of bounds. If n is 0, n-1 is SIZE_MAX and the very first access is out of bounds.
L4.explanation: Write it as `for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; )`, which tests before decrementing and terminates correctly at zero, including for n == 0.

L4.prompt_tpl: `unsigned char a = {a}, b = {b}; printf("%d %d", a + b, (unsigned char)(a + b));` What prints? Answer with the second printed value.
L4.answer: The first is the mathematical sum, because both operands are promoted to int before the addition: 300 for 200+100, 310 for 250+60. The second is that value modulo 256: 44 and 54 respectively.
L4.explanation: Narrow types do not wrap in expressions - they wrap on assignment back to the narrow type. This is why intermediate overflow bugs hide in code that looks 8-bit.

int x = 1, y = 2;
int& r = x;        // must be initialised; binds to x forever
r = y;             // assigns 2 TO x. It does NOT rebind r.
int* p = &x;       // may be null, may be reseated, must be dereferenced
p = &y;            // rebinds

void f(const std::string& s);          // no copy, no null, cannot be reseated
void g(std::string* s);                // null means "absent" - document it

const std::string& t = make_string();  // lifetime of the temporary is EXTENDED to t's scope

concepts.L1: A reference is an alias fixed at initialisation: it cannot be null, cannot be reseated, and needs no dereference syntax. A pointer is an object holding an address, so it can be null, reassigned, and stored in containers.
concepts.L2: Because a reference member cannot be reseated, a class containing one has its copy-assignment operator implicitly deleted - the compiler cannot write it. That is the usual reason a struct with a reference member mysteriously stops being assignable and cannot be stored in a vector.
concepts.L3: References are not a distinct run-time entity; the compiler is free to implement one as a pointer or as nothing at all after inlining, and sizeof(r) reports the size of the referent, not of a pointer. What they add is a static guarantee - a bound reference names a real object - so a function taking `const T&` need not check for null. The lifetime-extension rule for const references is the sharp edge: it works for a temporary bound directly at the declaration and does not survive being returned, so `const T& f() { return T(); }` compiles and dangles. Prefer references for parameters, pointers where absence is meaningful, and std::optional or a pointer where you must store the choice.

L4.prompt_tpl: `struct Holder {{ std::string& name; }}; std::vector<Holder> v; v.push_back(h1); v[0] = h2;` The last line fails to compile. Why?
L4.answer: Holder has a reference member, so its implicit copy-assignment operator is deleted - assigning a Holder would have to rebind name, which references cannot do. vector's element assignment therefore does not compile. Use a pointer, std::reference_wrapper, or store by value.
L4.explanation: std::reference_wrapper exists precisely for this: it is a rebindable, assignable, copyable reference-like object usable in containers.

L4.prompt_tpl: `int a = {a}, b = {b}; int& r = a; r = b; printf("%d %d", a, b);` What prints?
L4.answer: It prints b's value then b's value: for a=1, b=2 it prints '2 2'. `r = b` assigns through the reference into a; it does not make r refer to b.
L4.explanation: This is the whole difference from a pointer: there is no syntax for rebinding a reference, so every operation on r is an operation on a.

concepts.L1: Tie every resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime. Acquisition happens in the constructor, release in the destructor, and the language guarantees the destructor runs on every exit path from the scope, including exceptions.
concepts.L2: RAII is exception safety, not tidiness. The guarantee is that unwinding runs destructors for every fully constructed object, in reverse order - which is why a constructor that throws does not run its own destructor, and why partially constructed members are the one case you must reason about by hand.
concepts.L3: The compiler emits, for each scope, cleanup code on both the normal exit path and the unwinding path (personality routine plus LSDA tables), so a destructor call cannot be forgotten. Reverse order is required because later objects may depend on earlier ones. Two consequences follow. First, a throwing destructor during unwinding calls std::terminate, since the runtime cannot choose between two live exceptions - hence the implicit noexcept. Second, if a constructor throws, the object never existed, so its destructor does not run, though the destructors of already-constructed members and bases do - which is why each member should itself be an RAII type rather than a raw handle.

L4.prompt_tpl: `m.lock(); process(); m.unlock();` where process() can throw. What breaks, and what is the one-line fix?
L4.answer: If process() throws, the unlock never runs and the mutex stays locked forever, deadlocking every later acquirer. Replace the three lines with `std::lock_guard lk(m); process();` - the destructor unlocks on both the normal and the unwinding path.
L4.explanation: The same shape applies to every raw acquire/release pair: new/delete, fopen/fclose, malloc/free, BeginPaint/EndPaint. Wrap it once and never write the release again.

L4.prompt_tpl: Objects A, B, C are constructed in that order in a scope; C's constructor throws. Which destructors run, in what order?
L4.answer: B then A. C was never fully constructed so its destructor does not run, but any of C's own members that were fully constructed before the throw are destroyed. Fully constructed objects are destroyed in reverse construction order during unwinding.
L4.explanation: This is why a class should own resources through members that are themselves RAII types: the compiler then handles the partially constructed case for you.

concepts.t: The special member functions: rule of zero, three, five
concepts.L1: The compiler generates destructor, copy and move constructors and assignments unless you interfere. Declaring any of them changes what it generates for the others, so the correct counts are zero or five - never one.
concepts.L2: Writing an empty destructor for logging or a virtual one for a base class silently deletes the implicit move operations. Every move then resolves to a copy, and a container of such objects reallocates by deep-copying. The build stays green; the performance loss is invisible without a profiler.
concepts.L3: The generation rules are a compatibility ratchet. Copy operations predate move, so declaring a destructor or either copy operation suppresses the implicit move constructor and move assignment - the standard assumes a class with custom cleanup may not be memberwise-movable. Overload resolution then finds no move constructor and falls back to the copy constructor, because an rvalue binds happily to `const T&`. Nothing warns. The rule of zero avoids the whole area by making members responsible; when you cannot, declare all five, mark the move operations noexcept (vector's reallocation uses move_if_noexcept and will copy otherwise), and use `= default` so the compiler writes the bodies.

L4.prompt_tpl: A class holding a `std::vector<int>` of {n} elements gains `virtual ~Base() {{}}`. Profiling shows a large jump in memcpy time when these objects are pushed into a vector. Explain the causal chain.
L4.answer: Declaring the destructor suppressed the implicit move constructor and move assignment. Pushing an rvalue now selects the copy constructor, so each push deep-copies the vector's n elements, and every reallocation copies every element again instead of stealing pointers. Adding `Base(Base&&) noexcept = default;` and the matching move assignment restores it.
L4.explanation: Confirm with static_assert(std::is_move_constructible_v<T> && !std::is_copy_constructible_v<T>) on a test type, or check std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v, which is what vector actually queries.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why must a move constructor be marked noexcept for `std::vector<T>` to use it during reallocation?
L4.answer: vector offers the strong exception guarantee on reallocation: if anything throws, the original buffer must be intact. Moving destroys the source, so a throwing move would leave half the elements gone with no way to roll back. vector therefore calls move_if_noexcept, which selects the copy constructor unless the move is noexcept.
L4.explanation: This is the highest-value noexcept in C++ and it is easy to omit. is_nothrow_move_constructible is the trait to assert in a test.

concepts.t: Move semantics: rvalue references and std::move

L0.body:
std::vector<int> make();          // returns a prvalue

std::vector<int> a = make();      // no copy, no move: guaranteed elision (C++17)
std::vector<int> b = a;           // COPY: a is an lvalue
std::vector<int> c = std::move(a);// MOVE: std::move is just static_cast<vector<int>&&>(a)
// a is now valid but unspecified - assign to it or destroy it, nothing else

void sink(std::vector<int>&& v);  // binds only to rvalues
template <class T> void fwd(T&& t) { g(std::forward<T>(t)); }   // FORWARDING reference,
                                                                 // not an rvalue reference

concepts.L1: A move transfers ownership of a resource instead of duplicating it: the source's pointer is taken and the source is left in a destructible state. std::move only casts to an rvalue so that overload resolution selects the move overload.
concepts.L2: std::move on a const object silently does nothing: `const T&&` will not bind to the move constructor, so `T&` wins and you get a copy with no diagnostic. Every accidental const on a member or a range-for variable turns your moves back into copies.
concepts.L3: Value categories decide which overload binds. An lvalue has identity and cannot be assumed expendable, so it binds to `const T&` and gets copied. A prvalue or xvalue is expendable, so it binds to `T&&` and the move constructor can steal the source's heap pointer and null it out - O(1) instead of O(n). std::move manufactures an xvalue from an lvalue, which is a promise by you that the source is no longer needed. The library then defines the moved-from state as valid but unspecified, so the destructor and assignment are the only safe operations; implementations differ, and short-string optimisation in particular means a moved-from std::string may still hold its characters.

L4.prompt_tpl: `for (const auto& s : names) out.push_back(std::move(s));` with {n} strings. The author expects moves. What actually happens?
L4.answer: s is const, so std::move(s) yields a `const std::string&&`, which cannot bind to the move constructor taking `string&&`. Overload resolution falls back to the copy constructor taking `const string&`, and all n strings are deep-copied with no warning. Drop the const (use `auto&`) if the source may be consumed.
L4.explanation: This is the standard silent-copy bug. clang-tidy's performance-move-const-arg catches it; the compiler does not.

L4.prompt_tpl: `void take(std::string s); const std::string name = "{w}"; take(std::move(name));` Does this move or copy, and is there a diagnostic?
L4.answer: It copies, silently. std::move(name) yields `const std::string&&`, which will not bind to the move constructor's `std::string&&` parameter, so overload resolution falls back to the copy constructor taking `const std::string&`. No warning is emitted by default; -Wall does not catch it.
L4.explanation: std::move is a cast, not an operation, so it cannot fail loudly - it just produces a category the move constructor refuses. Every stray const on a member, a range-for variable or a return value turns moves back into copies with no diagnostic. Clang-tidy's performance-move-const-arg is the check that finds these.

L0.body:
auto u = std::make_unique<Widget>(args);   // sizeof(u) == 8 with the default deleter
auto s = std::make_shared<Widget>(args);   // ONE allocation: object + control block
std::weak_ptr<Widget> w = s;               // observes without owning; breaks cycles

if (auto locked = w.lock()) { locked->use(); }   // the only safe way to use a weak_ptr

std::unique_ptr<Widget> p = std::move(u);  // ownership transfer: unique_ptr is move-only
void take(std::unique_ptr<Widget>);        // a signature that documents ownership transfer
void use (const Widget&);                  // a signature that documents borrowing

concepts.L1: unique_ptr expresses sole ownership and compiles to a raw pointer with a destructor. shared_ptr expresses shared ownership with an atomically refcounted control block. weak_ptr observes without owning and is the cure for cycles.
concepts.L2: shared_ptr is the wrong default. Every copy is two atomic RMWs on a shared cache line, the control block doubles the pointer's size, and shared ownership makes lifetime unanalysable. Reach for unique_ptr plus references, and use shared_ptr only when ownership genuinely has no single home.
concepts.L3: unique_ptr is a class holding one pointer; with the default stateless deleter, empty base optimisation makes sizeof equal to a raw pointer and the destructor inlines to a delete, so the abstraction is free. shared_ptr is two pointers - to the object and to a control block holding the strong count, the weak count and the deleter - and copies do a lock-prefixed increment, contending on one cache line. make_shared fuses the two allocations into one, improving locality, with one caveat: that storage cannot be freed until the last weak_ptr goes away. Cycles are the structural failure - two objects holding shared_ptrs to each other never reach zero - and weak_ptr is the deliberate break.

L4.prompt_tpl: A tree where each node holds `shared_ptr<Node> children[{k}]` and each child holds `shared_ptr<Node> parent`. Memory grows monotonically. Diagnose and fix.
L4.answer: Parent and child hold strong references to each other, so neither strong count ever reaches zero and the whole subtree leaks - reference counting cannot collect cycles. Make the parent link a weak_ptr: children keep the parent alive only while the tree owns it, and lock() gives temporary access.
L4.explanation: The convention that works: ownership edges are shared_ptr and back-pointers are weak_ptr. A tracing GC would collect this without any change, which is exactly the refcounting-versus-tracing tradeoff.

L4.prompt_tpl: On x86-64 with the default deleter, what are sizeof(unique_ptr<T>), sizeof(shared_ptr<T>), and how many heap allocations does `make_shared<T>` perform versus `shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
L4.answer: unique_ptr: 8. shared_ptr: 16 (object pointer plus control-block pointer). make_shared performs one allocation for object and control block together; shared_ptr<T>(new T) performs two.
L4.explanation: A stateful deleter (a lambda with captures) enlarges unique_ptr, which is why the zero-overhead claim is specific to the stateless default.

concepts.t: Templates: instantiation, headers, and why the error messages are like that

L0.body:
template <class T>
T max_of(T a, T b) { return a < b ? b : a; }   // nothing is compiled until instantiated

max_of(1, 2);            // instantiates max_of<int>
max_of(std::string{}, std::string{});   // a second, unrelated function is emitted

template <class T> struct Wrapper { void f(); };
template <class T> void Wrapper<T>::f() { }    // definitions must be VISIBLE at the use site
                                               // - hence templates live in headers

template <class T> concept Ordered = requires (T a, T b) { { a < b } -> std::convertible_to<bool>; };
template <Ordered T> T max2(T a, T b) { return a < b ? b : a; }   // error at the CALL site

concepts.L1: A template is a code-generation pattern typechecked in two phases: names independent of the parameters are checked at definition, everything else at instantiation. Each distinct argument list produces a separate function or class.
concepts.L2: This is why templates go in headers and why compile times explode: the same body is parsed and instantiated in every translation unit that uses it, and the linker discards the duplicates afterwards. Explicit instantiation in one .cpp with `extern template` in the header buys the time back.
concepts.L3: Two-phase lookup splits checking: at definition time it resolves non-dependent names and syntax; at instantiation it substitutes and checks the rest. So `t.frobnicate()` is legal until someone instantiates with a type lacking frobnicate - and the diagnostic arrives from inside the body, several instantiations deep, listing the whole stack. That is the notorious error message: the constraint was never stated, so the compiler can only report where substitution failed. Concepts state the requirement on the parameter, so overload resolution rejects the call and names the unsatisfied requirement. The other consequence is code bloat: each instantiation is a distinct symbol with vague linkage.

L4.prompt_tpl: A template function is declared in a header and defined in a .cpp. It compiles, but linking a caller fails with 'undefined reference to {sym}'. Explain and give two fixes.
L4.answer: No code is generated for a template until it is instantiated, and instantiation requires the definition to be visible. The caller's translation unit sees only the declaration, so it emits a call to a symbol nobody defines. Fix by moving the definition into the header, or by explicitly instantiating the needed specialisations in the .cpp (`template int max_of<int>(int,int);`).
L4.explanation: Explicit instantiation is the right answer when the set of types is small and closed - it cuts compile time and keeps the body private.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does adding a concept turn a {n}-line template error message into one line?
L4.answer: Without a concept, the requirement exists only implicitly in the body, so the compiler discovers the failure during substitution and must report the entire instantiation stack that led there. A concept states the requirement on the parameter, so the candidate is removed during overload resolution and the diagnostic names the unsatisfied requirement at the call.
L4.explanation: This is the same principle as a type annotation on a function boundary: stating the contract locally makes failures local.
