concepts.t: Ownership and moves: who owns what, and when it drops

L0.body:
let s = String::from("hi");   // bindings are immutable by default
let mut t = s;                // MOVE: s is no longer usable; `mut` is on the binding
t.push('!');
// println!("{}", s);         // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s`

let a = 5;                    // i32 is Copy
let b = a;                    // copied, not moved
println!("{a} {b}");          // fine

let s = "shadowed";           // shadowing: a NEW binding reusing the name
{ let x = String::from("x"); }   // x is dropped here - end of scope, deterministically

concepts.L1: Every value has one owner. When the owner leaves scope the value is dropped, deterministically. Assignment or passing by value moves ownership unless the type implements Copy, after which the source binding is statically unusable.
concepts.L2: A move is not a run-time operation - it is a compile-time transfer of responsibility. The bytes are memcpy'd exactly as a copy would be; what changes is that the compiler stops allowing the source to be used and stops running its destructor. This is why moving a large struct is not automatically cheap.
concepts.L3: Ownership is enforced entirely at compile time by tracking, for each binding, whether it is currently initialised. A move marks the source as moved-out, so a later use is a use-of-moved-value error and drop is not emitted for it - if the move happens on only one branch, the compiler inserts a hidden drop flag to decide at run time. Copy is the opt-out for types whose bit pattern is self-contained: a type that is Copy cannot implement Drop, because duplicating something with a destructor would mean running it twice. Drop order is deterministic and specified: variables in reverse declaration order, struct fields in declaration order, which makes RAII in Rust total rather than conventional.

L4.prompt_tpl: `let v = vec![{a}, {b}]; let w = v; println!("{{:?}}", v);` What does the compiler say, and what would make it compile without cloning?
L4.answer: error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `v`. Vec is not Copy, so `let w = v` moves it. To compile without cloning, borrow instead: `let w = &v;`, which leaves v owning the data.
L4.explanation: Rust's suggested fix is often .clone(), which works and costs an allocation. Borrowing is usually the right answer, and the compiler proposes the expensive one because it is always correct.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can a type not implement both Copy and Drop?
L4.answer: Copy means duplicating the bits produces a second independent value, and both would then be dropped - the destructor would run twice on the same resource, causing a double free. The language forbids the combination outright.
L4.explanation: This is also why Copy is limited to types made of Copy fields: any owned heap pointer inside would create the same double-free.

concepts.t: Borrowing: &T, &mut T, and the two rules

L0.body:
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];

let r1 = &v;          // shared borrow
let r2 = &v;          // any number of these
println!("{r1:?} {r2:?}");   // r1 and r2 are dead after this line (NLL)

let m = &mut v;       // exclusive borrow - legal here only because r1/r2 are no longer used
m.push(4);

fn read(v: &Vec<i32>) -> usize { v.len() }        // borrow: caller keeps ownership
fn take(v: Vec<i32>) -> usize { v.len() }         // move: caller loses it

concepts.L1: A borrow is a reference that does not own. The checker enforces two rules: exclusive and shared borrows never coexist for the same value, and no reference outlives its referent. Since non-lexical lifetimes, a borrow ends at its last use.
concepts.L2: The rules are about aliasing, not about mutation. `&mut` means exclusive, not mutable - that is why it also forbids a second read-only borrow, and why the compiler can hand the optimiser a noalias annotation on every &mut, which C can only get from restrict.
concepts.L3: Borrow checking runs on MIR as a dataflow problem: for each borrow it computes the set of program points where the reference is live, then reports any point where an exclusive borrow's region overlaps another borrow of the same place. Non-lexical lifetimes made those regions end at the last use rather than the closing brace, which is why code that once required an inner scope now compiles unchanged. The pay-off is downstream: because &mut T is guaranteed unique, rustc emits LLVM noalias on it, so Rust gets by default what C gets only when a programmer writes restrict correctly. The cost: two mutable references into disjoint halves of a slice need an explicit API such as split_at_mut.

L4.prompt_tpl: `let mut v = vec![{a}, {b}, {c}]; let first = &v[0]; v.push({d}); println!("{{}}", first);` Why is it rejected, and what run-time bug is prevented?
L4.answer: push takes &mut v while the shared borrow `first` is still live at the println, so rule 1 is violated. The prevented bug is iterator invalidation: push may reallocate the buffer, and `first` would point into the freed allocation - a use-after-free that C++ compiles silently.
L4.explanation: Note the diagnosis order: the compiler rejects the aliasing, and dangling-freedom is a consequence. It does not model reallocation at all.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does the compiler reject a second `&v` while an `&mut v` is alive, given that reading cannot corrupt anything?
L4.answer: Because &mut means exclusive access, not merely permission to write. Allowing a concurrent reader would let it observe the value mid-modification and would invalidate the noalias guarantee the optimiser relies on. Exclusivity is the property being enforced; mutability is what it enables.
L4.explanation: Renaming &mut to 'unique reference' would have prevented years of confusion. Interior mutability (Cell, RefCell, Mutex) is the sanctioned way to mutate through a shared reference.

concepts.t: Lifetime annotations: what 'a does and does not mean
concepts.L1: A lifetime parameter is a name for a region of code over which a reference must remain valid. Annotations relate inputs to outputs so the checker can verify the relationship; they never extend or shorten an actual value's life.
concepts.L2: 'a on a return type does not keep anything alive. It constrains callers: the returned reference is usable only while the input it was derived from is. Fighting the borrow checker with more annotations is nearly always a sign that the design should own the data, not borrow it.
concepts.L3: Lifetimes exist only for the checker. The compiler infers regions for every reference, and annotations are constraints in that inference - `longest<'a>` says both arguments and the result share one region, so the caller's region is intersected down to the shorter input's, and using the result after that input dies is an error at the call site. Elision covers the three common shapes so most signatures need no annotation, and the &self rule is why methods returning references to fields are almost always elidable. After borrow checking, all of it is erased: MIR carries no lifetimes into codegen, so there is no run-time representation to inspect, and a lifetime can never be branched on.

L4.prompt_tpl: `fn make<'a>() -> &'a str {{ let s = String::from("{w}"); &s }}` fails to compile. Explain what 'a would have to mean for this to work.
L4.answer: 'a is chosen by the caller, so the function promises a reference valid for a region it does not control, while s is dropped at the end of the body. For it to work, 'a would have to extend the local's lifetime - which annotations cannot do. Return the owned String, or a &'static str, or take a borrowed input to derive from.
L4.explanation: This is the clearest demonstration that annotations describe rather than create. The error E0515 says 'returns a value referencing data owned by the current function'.

L4.prompt_tpl: Write out the fully annotated signature that elision produces for `fn parse(&self, input: &str) -> &str`.
L4.answer: fn parse<'a, 'b>(&'a self, input: &'b str) -> &'a str. Each input gets its own lifetime; because &self is present, the output takes self's lifetime - not the input's.
L4.explanation: This is the elision rule that most surprises people: a parser method returning a slice of `input` will NOT compile under elision, because the output was tied to self. You must annotate it explicitly.

concepts.t: Traits, impl blocks, and generic bounds
concepts.L1: Traits declare behaviour a type can implement, from anywhere in the program rather than inside the type's definition. Generic bounds constrain a parameter to types implementing them, checked once at the definition rather than per instantiation.
concepts.L2: Unlike C++ templates, a generic function is typechecked against its bounds alone, so calling a method you did not require is an error at the definition, not at some caller's instantiation. That is parametricity restored, and it is why Rust generic errors point at your code and template errors point at the library's.
concepts.L3: A bound is a proof obligation discharged at the call site: the compiler finds an impl of Shape for the concrete T, then monomorphises the function with the method calls statically bound and inlinable. Because checking happens at the definition, `fn f<T: Shape>(t: T) { t.other() }` is rejected immediately unless `other` is in the bounds - the opposite of C++'s substitution-time checking. Coherence is enforced by the orphan rule: an impl is allowed only if the trait or the type is local to your crate, which guarantees at most one impl of a trait for a type across the whole program and so makes method resolution unambiguous. The workaround, when you own neither, is the newtype wrapper.

L4.prompt_tpl: You want `impl Display for Vec<{T}>` in your crate. It fails with E0117. Why, and what is the standard workaround?
L4.answer: Both Display and Vec are foreign to your crate, so the orphan rule rejects the impl - otherwise two crates could each provide one and the compiler could not choose. The workaround is a newtype: `struct Wrapper(Vec<T>);` which is local, so `impl Display for Wrapper` is allowed.
L4.explanation: Coherence is what lets Rust resolve trait methods globally and unambiguously. The cost is exactly this friction, and newtype is the sanctioned answer.

L4.prompt_tpl: When would you choose `&dyn Shape` over `impl Shape` / `<T: Shape>` for a collection of {n} shapes?
L4.answer: Use dyn when the collection must hold several different concrete types at once - a Vec<Box<dyn Shape>> is heterogeneous, a Vec<T> is not - or when you want one compiled copy instead of one per type, to cut binary size and compile time. Use generics when the type is uniform and per-call inlining matters.
L4.explanation: The decision is heterogeneity first, code size second, speed third. Dynamic dispatch's direct cost is small; the lost inlining is the real difference.

concepts.t: Pattern matching and enums with data
concepts.L1: A Rust enum is a tagged union whose variants carry data. match destructures it, arms are tried in order, guards refine them, and the compiler requires the set of arms to cover every variant.
concepts.L2: Matching on a value moves it. `match msg { Msg::Write(s) => ... }` moves the String out and leaves msg unusable; matching on `&msg` binds s as a reference instead. This is match ergonomics, and it is the difference between a compile error and code that quietly consumes its input.
concepts.L3: The compiler lowers a match to a decision tree on the discriminant, so dispatch is a jump table rather than a chain of comparisons, and exhaustiveness is decided with Maranget's usefulness algorithm: an arm is useful if some value reaches it, and the match is exhaustive if adding a wildcard arm would be useless. Binding modes then follow the scrutinee: matching a place expression of reference type shifts bindings to `ref` automatically, which is what lets `if let Some(x) = &opt` give `&T` without a single explicit ref. Guards are evaluated after the pattern matches and cannot bind new names, so they do not participate in exhaustiveness - a guarded arm never counts as covering its variant.

L4.prompt_tpl: `match opt {{ Some(s) => use_it(s), None => {{}} }}` then `println!("{{:?}}", opt);` fails. Fix it in two different ways.
L4.answer: The match moved the String out of opt, so opt is partially moved and unusable afterwards. Fix by matching on a reference (`match &opt`) if use_it can take &String, or by using `opt.as_ref()`; alternatively use `ref s` in the pattern. If you really want to consume it, move the println earlier.
L4.explanation: Since the 2021 edition, match ergonomics handles the common case automatically once you match on &opt - the binding becomes &String with no ref keyword.

L4.prompt_tpl: Given `enum E {{ A, B, C }}`, a match has arms for A and B and a guarded arm `C if n > {n} => ...`. Does it compile?
L4.answer: No: error E0004, non-exhaustive patterns - a guarded arm never counts as covering its variant
L4.explanation: Exhaustiveness is a static property, and a guard is an arbitrary run-time expression. This is a good thing: the alternative would be a silent fallthrough with no arm to run.
options: No: error E0004, non-exhaustive patterns - a guarded arm never counts as covering its variant
Yes: the guard is evaluated at run time, and the compiler treats the arm as covering C
Yes, with a warning: rustc accepts it and emits an unreachable_patterns lint for the guarded arm

concepts.L1: Errors are values: Result<T, E> and Option<T> are ordinary enums, so a fallible call returns a value you must inspect. `?` is early return plus an automatic From conversion of the error type.
concepts.L2: The From conversion inside `?` is the part that does the work. It is why a function returning Box<dyn Error> can absorb io::Error and ParseIntError with no glue, and why writing a custom error enum with #[from] impls (thiserror) makes the operator work across your whole crate.
concepts.L3: `expr?` desugars to a match on the Try trait: on the success branch it evaluates to the contained value, and on the failure branch it returns Err(From::from(e)) from the enclosing function. Two consequences follow. First, the enclosing return type must be a Try type whose error is reachable by From from the callee's error, which is why mixing Option and Result needs an explicit ok_or or ok. Second, because the error is converted rather than boxed blindly, an application can define one error enum per layer and let `?` walk values up, preserving the source chain Error::source exposes. Unlike an exception, nothing unwinds: every propagation point is a visible character.

L4.prompt_tpl: `fn f() -> Option<i32> {{ let s = std::fs::read_to_string("{p}")?; s.trim().parse().ok() }}` does not compile. Why?
L4.answer: read_to_string returns Result<String, io::Error>, but the function returns Option<i32>, and ? cannot convert a Result's error into None - there is no such From impl and discarding the error would be silent. Either change the return type to Result, or write `.ok()?` to explicitly discard the error first.
L4.explanation: The compiler suggests exactly this. The design intent is that throwing away an error must be a deliberate, visible act.

L4.prompt_tpl: A library function calls .unwrap() on a Result in {n} places. Why is that a defect in a library but acceptable in a binary's main?
L4.answer: unwrap panics, which aborts or unwinds the caller's thread and removes the caller's ability to handle the failure - a library must not make that decision for the application. In main, panicking IS the error handling: the process exits with a message, and there is no caller to deprive.
L4.explanation: The middle ground for a library is expect("reason") for genuinely impossible states, documented as such, plus a real error type for everything else.

concepts.L1: A Python name is a binding in a namespace, not a storage location. Assignment rebinds the name; it never copies the object. Argument passing binds the parameter name to the caller's object, so mutation is visible to the caller and rebinding is not.
concepts.L2: A default argument is evaluated once, when def executes, and the resulting object is stored on the function - so a mutable default is shared state across every call. The idiom is `def f(x, acc=None)` with the real default constructed inside the body.
concepts.L3: Every Python object lives on the heap with a refcount and a type pointer, and a name is an entry in a dict (module globals, an instance __dict__) or a slot in the fast-locals array of a frame. `b = a` copies a pointer and bumps a refcount; `b.append(3)` calls a method on the shared object. This single model explains the whole cluster of surprises: mutable defaults (the default object is stored in func.__defaults__ at definition), aliasing bugs (two names, one list), and the fact that `def f(x): x = []` cannot affect the caller while `def f(x): x.append(1)` can. copy.copy and copy.deepcopy exist because there is no implicit copying anywhere in the language.

L4.explanation: Mutation propagates, rebinding does not. That one sentence is the whole of Python's parameter-passing semantics.

concepts.L1: An iterator is any object with __next__ raising StopIteration when finished. A generator is an iterator the compiler builds from a function containing yield, suspending the frame at each yield and resuming it on the next call.
concepts.L2: Generators are single-use. Passing one to two consumers, or looping over it twice, silently gives the second consumer nothing - no error, just an empty result. If you need to re-iterate, keep the underlying iterable, or materialise it into a list and accept the memory.
concepts.L3: A generator object holds its frame - locals, instruction pointer, and value stack - on the heap rather than the C stack, so suspension is just storing the offset of the next bytecode and returning. Resuming restores the frame and continues, which is why locals survive across yields and why an unclosed generator keeps everything it references alive. The cost model follows: memory is O(1) in the number of items rather than O(n), and work is done only as far as the consumer pulls - so `next(g)` on an infinite generator terminates. Exhaustion is permanent because the frame is marked finished; that is also why a generator's `return value` becomes StopIteration.value rather than a yielded item.

L4.prompt_tpl: `g = (x for x in range({n})); print(sum(g), sum(g), max(g, default=-1))` What prints? Answer with the first value printed.

L4.explanation: The absence of an error is the danger: a function that takes an iterable and traverses it twice silently produces wrong results when handed a generator.

L4.explanation: Dropping the brackets is the single highest-yield memory change in Python. Note it is only a win when the consumer is streaming - sorted() or len() must materialise anyway.

concepts.L1: __slots__ declares a fixed set of attribute names, replacing the per-instance dictionary with class-level descriptors over a compact array. Instances shrink substantially and attribute access becomes an offset load instead of a dict lookup.
concepts.L2: The saving evaporates if any subclass omits __slots__, because that subclass reintroduces __dict__ and every instance carries both. It also removes weakref support unless you add __weakref__ explicitly, which quietly breaks caches and observer registries built on weak references.
concepts.L3: A normal instance stores attributes in a dict reached through a pointer in the object header; CPython 3.3+ shares the key table across instances of a class, but each instance still owns a values array and the dict object. __slots__ instead allocates the values inline in the object and installs one descriptor per name on the class, so `p.x` is a fixed-offset load rather than a hash lookup - modestly faster, materially smaller. Measure with sys.getsizeof on the instance plus its __dict__; savings for small objects are commonly 30-50%. The costs are rigidity - no monkey-patching, no attributes added at run time - and awkward interactions with inheritance and pickling.

import asyncio

async def fetch(i):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)          # yields control to the loop
    return i

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(i) for i in range(10)))   # ~1s total, not 10
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:      # 3.11+: structured
        tg.create_task(fetch(1))

asyncio.run(main())

fetch(1)             # returns a coroutine object and runs NOTHING (RuntimeWarning)
time.sleep(1)        # inside a coroutine: blocks the WHOLE loop and every other task
L0.cloze:
# Calling an `async def` function returns a {{c1::coroutine}} object; it runs only when
# {{c2::awaited}} or scheduled as a Task.
# `await` {{c3::suspends}} the coroutine and returns control to the {{c4::event loop}}.
# A blocking call inside a coroutine stalls {{c5::every}} task on that loop -
# offload it with asyncio.to_thread or run_in_executor.

concepts.L1: An async def function is a coroutine factory: calling it builds a coroutine that does nothing until awaited or scheduled. await suspends at that point and hands control back to a single-threaded event loop that resumes whichever coroutine is ready.
concepts.L2: Concurrency comes from awaiting, not from async. `await a(); await b()` is strictly sequential; only gather, TaskGroup or create_task overlap them. And one synchronous blocking call - requests.get, a CPU loop, time.sleep - freezes every task on the loop, because there is exactly one thread.
concepts.L3: An async def body compiles to a coroutine object built on the generator machinery: each await is a suspension point where the frame is saved and control returns to the loop, an epoll poll plus a ready queue. Because suspension only happens at an explicit await, the code between two awaits is atomic with respect to other tasks - no locks needed for it - and because there is one thread, any operation that does not yield holds the loop for its whole duration. That is the whole performance model: only as good as the least cooperative call. It also explains the coloured-function constraint - await is legal only inside a function the compiler transformed, so async propagates up every caller.

L4.prompt_tpl: `async def f(): await asyncio.sleep(1)` - compare total wall time for `for _ in range({n}): await f()` versus `await asyncio.gather(*(f() for _ in range({n})))`. Answer with the wall time in seconds of the sequential loop.
L4.answer: The loop takes about n seconds - each await runs to completion before the next starts. gather takes about 1 second, because all n coroutines are scheduled as tasks and their sleeps overlap on the single loop.
L4.explanation: await means 'wait for this'. It is a synchronisation point, not a concurrency primitive; the concurrency comes from having several tasks scheduled at once.

L4.prompt_tpl: An asyncio web service adds `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac(...)` costing {ms} ms per request inside a handler. p99 latency across all endpoints collapses. Explain and fix.
L4.answer: The hash is synchronous CPU work with no await inside it, so it occupies the single event-loop thread for its full duration and every other task - including already-connected clients - waits. Move it off the loop with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` or a ProcessPoolExecutor.
L4.explanation: The failure is global, not local: the affected latency is on endpoints that never call the hash. That signature - unrelated endpoints slowing down together - is the fingerprint of a blocked event loop.

sections.note: the syntax is small; the performance model is the entire subject

concepts.t: Kernel launch: __global__ and the triple chevron
concepts.L1: __global__ marks a function launched from the host and executed by every thread of a grid. The triple chevron supplies grid dimensions, block dimensions, dynamic shared memory and a stream. Launch is asynchronous - control returns to the host immediately.
concepts.L2: Because launches are asynchronous and errors are sticky, a kernel that faults reports at the NEXT CUDA call, which may be a memcpy hundreds of lines later. Any error checking that does not call cudaGetLastError immediately after the launch and then synchronise is attributing failures to the wrong line.
concepts.L3: The chevron syntax is handled by nvcc, which rewrites it into cudaLaunchKernel with a packed argument array and splits the file into host code (handed to the host compiler) and device code (compiled to PTX and then SASS, either ahead of time for a listed -arch or JIT-compiled from embedded PTX at load). Asynchrony is what makes GPUs usable: the host queues work into a stream and continues, so launch overhead of a few microseconds can be overlapped with the previous kernel. It is also why timing a kernel with host clocks around the launch measures nothing, and why every error report needs an explicit synchronisation to be attributed correctly.

L4.prompt_tpl: Launch a kernel over n = {n} elements with 256 threads per block. How many blocks, how many threads total, and how many threads take the early-exit branch? Answer with the number of blocks.
L4.answer: blocks = ceil(n/256). For n=1000: 4 blocks, 1024 threads, 24 idle. For n=1000000: 3907 blocks, 999,992... more precisely 3907*256 = 1,000,192 threads, 192 idle. For n=1048576: exactly 4096 blocks, 1,048,576 threads, none idle.
L4.explanation: The guard `if (i < n)` exists because the grid is rounded up. Omitting it writes past the end of the buffer - the most common first CUDA bug.

L4.prompt_tpl: `kernel<<<{b}, 2048>>>(...)` returns no error from the launch line but produces no output. Diagnose.
L4.answer: 2048 exceeds the hardware maximum of 1024 threads per block, so the launch fails with cudaErrorInvalidConfiguration. The launch statement itself returns void, so the error is only visible via cudaGetLastError() immediately afterwards - which the code never calls, so the kernel silently never ran.
L4.explanation: Wrap every launch in a macro that calls cudaGetLastError and cudaDeviceSynchronize in debug builds. Also run under compute-sanitizer, which reports it directly.

concepts.t: Thread indexing and the grid-stride loop
concepts.L1: threadIdx is the thread's position within its block, blockIdx the block's within the grid, blockDim and gridDim their sizes. Combining them gives a global index; a grid-stride loop makes one kernel correct for any n and any grid size.
concepts.L2: Which index you map to threadIdx.x decides your memory bandwidth. Adjacent threads must touch adjacent addresses, so for a row-major matrix threadIdx.x must index the column. Transposing that one mapping can cost an order of magnitude while both versions are equally correct.
concepts.L3: Threads are dispatched in warps of 32 consecutive threadIdx.x values, and the memory system services a warp's loads by coalescing them into the smallest set of 32-byte sectors that covers the requested addresses. If thread t accesses base + 4t, one warp's 128 bytes fall in four sectors - fully coalesced. If it accesses base + 4*t*stride, the same warp touches up to 32 separate sectors, so it moves up to eight times the bytes. Nothing about the code looks different. The grid-stride loop is the second habit: by decoupling the number of threads from n, the same kernel handles any input, allows configurations tuned for occupancy, and lets each thread reuse register state across iterations.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel accesses `a[threadIdx.x * {s}]` with 4-byte floats. How many 32-byte sectors does one warp of 32 threads touch, versus stride 1? Answer with the number of 32-byte sectors the warp touches.
L4.answer: Stride 1: the warp covers 128 contiguous bytes = 4 sectors. Stride 2: 256 bytes covered but only half used = 8 sectors, so twice the traffic for the same useful data. Stride 32: each thread's element is 128 bytes from the next, so all 32 fall in distinct sectors = 32 sectors, eight times the traffic of stride 1.
L4.explanation: This is the whole coalescing story in one calculation. Confirm on real code with ncu's gld_efficiency / l1tex sector metrics.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why write a grid-stride loop instead of `if (i < n)` when n is known to be {n}?
L4.answer: It decouples grid size from problem size: the same kernel runs correctly with a grid sized for occupancy rather than for n, works for n larger than the maximum grid, allows one thread to amortise setup across several elements, and makes the kernel debuggable with a single block. The if-guard version forces one thread per element.
L4.explanation: It also makes results reproducible across launch configurations, which matters when a reduction's ordering affects floating-point results.

concepts.t: Memory spaces: global, shared, registers, constant
concepts.L1: A CUDA thread sees a hierarchy: registers (per thread), shared memory (per block, software-managed scratchpad), L1/L2, and global device memory. Shared memory is the one an ordinary CPU programmer has no analogue for, and it is where most optimisation happens.
concepts.L2: Shared memory is banked into 32 four-byte-wide banks. Threads of a warp hitting different addresses in the same bank serialise, so a 32x32 float tile indexed by column makes every access a 32-way conflict. Padding the row to 33 floats shifts each row by one bank and removes it entirely.
concepts.L3: Global memory is off-chip DRAM at 400-800 cycles of latency; shared memory is on-chip SRAM at roughly 20-30, partitioned per streaming multiprocessor and split with the L1 cache. The tiling pattern exists to exploit that: load a tile cooperatively from global with coalesced accesses, __syncthreads, then read it many times from shared in whatever order the algorithm wants. Registers are faster but scarce: too many per thread reduces how many blocks fit on an SM (occupancy) and past the limit spills to local memory, which is global memory with a per-thread layout. Bank conflicts are the shared-memory analogue of uncoalesced access, and the padding trick works because bank = (address/4) mod 32.

L4.prompt_tpl: `__shared__ float s[32][{w}];` accessed as `s[threadIdx.x][k]` by a warp of 32 threads with fixed k. How many-way is the bank conflict for w = 32 and for w = 33?
L4.answer: With w=32, thread t addresses element 32t + k, so bank = (32t + k) mod 32 = k for every thread - all 32 threads hit one bank, a 32-way conflict serialised into 32 accesses. With w=33, bank = (33t + k) mod 32 = (t + k) mod 32, which is distinct for every t - no conflict.
L4.explanation: One padding element removes a 32x slowdown. This is the single most valuable arithmetic fact in shared-memory programming.

L4.prompt_tpl: A kernel using {r} registers per thread runs at low occupancy. Name two ways to raise occupancy and the cost of each.
L4.answer: Cap registers with __launch_bounds__ or -maxrregcount, which lets more blocks fit per SM but spills the excess to local memory, adding global-memory traffic. Or reduce shared memory per block, which frees the other occupancy-limiting resource but usually means smaller tiles and less reuse. Occupancy is not the goal - latency hiding is; a low-occupancy kernel with high ILP can be faster.
L4.explanation: Use the occupancy calculator or ncu to see which resource is the limiter before changing anything. Volkov's work showed high occupancy is neither necessary nor sufficient for peak throughput.

if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0) heavy_a();     // half the warp masked off
else                      heavy_b();     // then the other half: cost = A + B

__syncthreads();          // barrier for the BLOCK. Every thread must reach the SAME one.
if (threadIdx.x < 16) { __syncthreads(); }   // UNDEFINED: not all threads reach it

__syncwarp();             // since Volta, warps can diverge independently: sync explicitly
int mask = __ballot_sync(0xffffffff, pred);  // warp-level primitives need an explicit mask

concepts.L1: Threads execute in warps of 32 under one instruction stream. When threads in a warp take different branches the hardware executes both paths with inactive lanes masked, so cost is additive. __syncthreads is a barrier across the whole block, not the warp.
concepts.L2: Divergence is a per-warp phenomenon, so `if (i < n/2)` costs nothing when the split falls on a warp boundary and doubles the cost when it falls inside a warp. Restructuring data so that a branch is uniform across each 32-thread group is often a bigger win than removing the branch.
concepts.L3: Pre-Volta hardware kept one program counter per warp, so the compiler reconverged divergent threads at a post-dominator and lockstep assumptions were safe. Volta introduced independent thread scheduling with a PC per thread, which makes some previously working code wrong: threads may not reconverge, so warp-level exchange (shuffle, ballot, vote) needs an explicit mask and __syncwarp. __syncthreads is a block barrier implemented in hardware; the requirement that every thread reach the same barrier is why calling it inside a divergent if is undefined - some threads wait forever, or different threads arrive at textually different barriers and the block silently produces wrong results.

L4.prompt_tpl: Branch A costs {a} cycles, branch B costs {b}. What is the cost per warp when the predicate is `threadIdx.x % 2 == 0` versus `threadIdx.x / 32 % 2 == 0`? Answer with the cost per warp in cycles for the first predicate.
L4.answer: The first predicate splits every warp, so each warp executes both paths: a + b cycles. The second is uniform within each warp (it varies only across warps), so each warp takes just one branch: max(a, b) at worst, a or b for any given warp - no divergence penalty at all.
L4.explanation: Identical work, identical results, very different cost. Restructuring so predicates are warp-uniform is the standard divergence fix.

prereqs: Memory spaces: global, shared, registers, constant

concepts.L1: Device memory is allocated with cudaMalloc and filled by an explicit copy across PCIe or NVLink. Copies and kernels issued into the same stream are ordered; separate streams overlap, which is how transfer is hidden behind computation.
concepts.L2: cudaMemcpyAsync on ordinary pageable memory is not asynchronous - the driver must stage through an internal pinned buffer first, so it blocks anyway. The async path only exists for memory allocated with cudaMallocHost or registered with cudaHostRegister, and forgetting that is why overlap often fails to materialise.
concepts.L3: The DMA engine can only read host memory the OS has promised not to move, so a transfer from pageable memory is a staged copy into a driver-owned pinned buffer, then a DMA. Pinning removes the staging, freeing the host thread and letting a copy engine run concurrently with the SMs. Streams are the ordering primitive built on that: operations in one stream form a sequence, and separate streams are independent, so a chunked pipeline (copy chunk i+1 while computing chunk i) can approach hiding the entire transfer time. Unified memory replaces this with demand paging - fine when access is sparse or the working set fits, but a page-fault storm is far slower than a bulk copy.

L4.prompt_tpl: A workload transfers {mb} MB at 12 GB/s over PCIe and computes for {ms} ms. What is the total time serially, and with a two-stream pipeline of many chunks? Answer with the serial total in milliseconds.
L4.answer: Transfer time = mb/12000 seconds; for 1200 MB that is 100 ms. Serial total = transfer + compute (200 ms for 1200 MB + 100 ms). With deep chunked overlap the total approaches max(transfer, compute) plus one chunk of latency, so about 100 ms - a 2x speedup when the two are balanced.
L4.explanation: Overlap can never beat max(copy, compute); if transfer dominates, the fix is to move less data or keep it resident, not to add streams.

L4.prompt_tpl: Code issues cudaMemcpyAsync from a `malloc`ed buffer, then a kernel, then cudaMemcpyAsync back, all on stream {s}, and sees no overlap in the profiler. Why?
L4.answer: Two reasons. The host buffer is pageable, so the async copies degrade to synchronous staged copies. And all three operations are in the same stream, which is ordered by definition - overlap requires at least two streams working on different chunks. Allocate with cudaMallocHost and pipeline across two or more streams.

L0.body:
$ gcc -E main.c -o main.i     # 1. preprocess: #include textually pasted, macros expanded
$ gcc -S main.i -o main.s     # 2. compile:    C -> assembly
$ gcc -c main.s -o main.o     # 3. assemble:   assembly -> ELF object with a symbol table
$ gcc main.o util.o -o app    # 4. link:       resolve symbols, lay out sections

$ wc -l main.c main.i         # the preprocessor output is often 100x the source
$ nm -C main.o                # T = defined text symbol, U = undefined (needs the linker)
$ readelf -S app              # .text .rodata .data .bss and the rest

concepts.L1: A build runs four separable programs. The preprocessor produces one translation unit per source file by textual inclusion, the compiler emits assembly, the assembler emits a relocatable object with a symbol table, and the linker resolves symbols across objects into an executable.
concepts.L2: The compiler never sees more than one translation unit, so it cannot check anything across files - a mismatched declaration in C links happily and corrupts the stack at run time. Type safety across TUs is C++'s name mangling, not the linker's, which is why C has none.
concepts.L3: Separating the stages is what makes separate compilation possible: each .c becomes a .o with a symbol table listing what it defines (T, D, B) and what it needs (U), and the linker matches them by name only. It resolves the references, assigns final addresses, applies relocations, and merges sections. Nothing about types survives into the object file in C, so `extern int f(void);` in one file and `double f(double)` in another link cleanly and go wrong at run time. Knowing where a build broke is mostly a matter of knowing which of the four stages emitted the message: an unknown identifier is the compiler, an undefined reference is the linker, and a missing header is the preprocessor.

L4.prompt_tpl: Classify each error: (a) 'fatal error: {h}: No such file or directory', (b) 'undefined reference to `foo`', (c) 'implicit declaration of function `bar`'. Which stage, and what fixes each?
L4.answer: (a) Preprocessor: the header is not on the include path - add -I or install the -dev package. (b) Linker: some object or library defining foo was not given - add the .o or -lfoo, in the right order. (c) Compiler: no declaration was visible - include the right header (in C99+ it is an error, and calling it anyway is UB).
L4.explanation: Reading the stage off the message is the fastest debugging skill in C and C++ builds, and it is entirely mechanical.

L4.prompt_tpl: File a.c has `int counter;` and b.c has `extern long counter;` (note: long). Both compile and the program links. What happens at run time on x86-64?
L4.answer: They resolve to one symbol at one address. b.c reads and writes 8 bytes where a.c reserved 4, so writes through the long clobber the adjacent 4 bytes of whatever the linker placed next, and reads see garbage in the high half. No stage diagnoses it, because the object file records only a name and a size.
L4.explanation: This is exactly what -fno-common (the default since GCC 10) and link-time type checking in C++ address. In C the only defence is a shared header declaring the symbol once.

concepts.t: Incremental builds and the dependency graph

L0.body:
# Make rebuilds a target when a prerequisite is NEWER (mtime), not when content changed.
app: main.o util.o
	$(CC) $^ -o $@

# Headers are invisible to make unless you generate the dependencies:
CFLAGS += -MMD -MP          # emit main.d listing every header main.c included
-include $(OBJS:.o=.d)

$ make -j$(nproc)           # parallelism comes from the graph, so the graph must be right
$ ccache gcc -c main.c      # content-hash cache: survives a clean, unlike mtime
$ ninja -t deps             # ninja stores the same header deps in a binary log

concepts.L1: An incremental build is a DAG walk: rebuild a target if any prerequisite is newer. Correctness depends entirely on the graph being complete, and the edges everyone forgets are the ones from object files to the headers they included.
concepts.L2: A build with missing header dependencies is not slow, it is wrong: you change a struct, only some translation units rebuild, and the resulting binary mixes two layouts of the same type. The symptom is a crash that disappears after `make clean`, which is why that ritual exists.
concepts.L3: Make's model is mtime comparison, which is cheap and has two failure modes: an incomplete graph under-builds, a touched file over-builds. -MMD makes the compiler emit the exact list of headers it opened, and -MP adds phony targets so that deleting a header does not break the build - together they close the first hole mechanically. The under-build failure is the dangerous one because it produces an ODR violation across objects: one .o compiled against the old struct layout and another against the new, linked into a binary where field offsets disagree. Content-addressed systems (Bazel, ccache) replace timestamps with hashes and get cache hits across branches and machines.

L4.prompt_tpl: A Makefile has no header dependencies. A developer adds a field to a struct in `types.h` and rebuilds with `make -j{j}`. The program crashes; `make clean && make` fixes it. Explain precisely.
L4.answer: Only the .c files that themselves changed were recompiled. Objects compiled before the edit still use the old struct layout, so two objects disagree on sizeof and on every field offset after the new one. Linking them produces a binary where one function writes at the new offset and another reads at the old - an ODR violation the linker cannot see. Adding -MMD -MP and -include of the .d files fixes it permanently.
L4.explanation: 'make clean fixes it' is the diagnostic signature of a missing dependency edge. It is never the right long-term answer.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does ccache still hit after `make clean`, when make itself must rebuild everything?
L4.answer: make decides by mtime, and clean deleted the outputs, so every target looks out of date. ccache decides by hashing the preprocessed source plus the compiler and flags, so the deleted object's content key is unchanged and it replays the cached result instead of running the compiler.
L4.explanation: Same insight scaled up is what Bazel and other content-addressed systems do for the whole graph, including across machines via a remote cache.

-O0   no optimisation, fast compiles, faithful debugging      (never ship this)
-O1   cheap passes;  -O2  the standard shipping level
-O3   adds aggressive inlining and vectorisation - sometimes SLOWER (I-cache)
-Os   optimise for size;  -Oz (clang) harder;  -Og  optimise but keep debugging usable

-g            DWARF debug info. Independent of -O: it does NOT slow the program down.
-DNDEBUG      compiles out assert()  - the default in CMake's Release build

concepts.L1: -O selects how much the optimiser is allowed to do, -g adds debug information without changing the generated code, -march targets an instruction set, and -DNDEBUG removes assertions. Ship -O2 -g and keep the symbols.
concepts.L2: -g does not make the program slower - it adds sections the loader never maps into the hot path - so stripping symbols from a release build buys nothing but unreadable stack traces. Separate them with objcopy --only-keep-debug if binary size matters.
concepts.L3: -O2 enables roughly a hundred named passes; -O3 adds more aggressive inlining, loop unrolling and vectorisation, which enlarges code and can lose more to I-cache pressure than it gains - which is why large binaries often measure -O2 as faster. -march=native does two things at once: it permits instructions the build machine supports (AVX-512, FMA) and tunes scheduling for it, so the binary is no longer portable; enabling FMA also changes results, since GCC contracts a*b+c into one fused instruction with a single rounding. -ffast-math goes further and licenses reassociation, so sums of floats may differ run to run under vectorisation - defensible for graphics, rarely for finance.

L4.answer: Release builds define NDEBUG, which makes assert expand to nothing - so the whole call to queue_pop disappears along with it. Never put a side effect inside assert; call the function, store the result, then assert on the variable.

concepts.t: Translation units, declarations, definitions, and the ODR
concepts.L1: A translation unit is what the compiler actually sees: one source file after preprocessing. Declarations may repeat; definitions may not, except for classes, templates and inline functions, which may appear once per TU if every copy is identical.
concepts.L2: ODR violations are ill-formed with no diagnostic required. Two TUs compiled with different -D flags or different struct definitions link cleanly, the linker keeps one arbitrary copy of each inline function, and half the program runs against a layout the other half does not share.
concepts.L3: Inline functions and template instantiations are emitted into every object file that uses them, with COMDAT (vague) linkage that tells the linker to discard all but one copy. That mechanism makes header-only code possible, and it is also the hole: the linker deduplicates by mangled name, not by content, so if two TUs saw different definitions of `inline int f()` - because a macro or #ifdef differed - it keeps whichever it encountered first and the other TU's expectations are silently violated. The failure is a wrong field offset or a function body from the wrong build, appearing far from the cause. gold and lld's --detect-odr-violations and ASan's odr_indicator catch some of it.

L4.prompt_tpl: a.cpp is compiled with -DFEATURE and b.cpp without it. A header defines `struct S {{ int x; #ifdef FEATURE int y; #endif }};` and an inline function operating on S. The program links. What happens?
L4.answer: The two TUs have different definitions of S - different sizeof and different layout - which is an ODR violation. Objects allocated in one TU and used in the other read and write past or short of the real fields, and the linker keeps only one copy of the inline function, so one TU runs code compiled against the wrong layout. No diagnostic is required and none is issued.
L4.explanation: This is the single most common cause of 'works in one build configuration, crashes in another'. Flags that change type layout must be global to the build, not per-target.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why may a class definition appear in {n} translation units while a function definition may not?
L4.answer: A class definition emits no symbol - it is type information the compiler needs in every TU that uses the type - so repeating it costs nothing at link time provided all copies are identical. A non-inline function definition emits a symbol with external linkage, and two would be a duplicate-symbol link error. inline exists precisely to move a function into the first category via COMDAT linkage.
L4.explanation: This is what `inline` actually means, and why it is the keyword you need for header-defined functions even when you do not care whether the compiler inlines them.

concepts.t: Static and dynamic libraries, and why link order matters

L0.body:
$ ar rcs libutil.a a.o b.o                      # static: an archive of object files
$ gcc -shared -fPIC -o libutil.so a.o b.o       # dynamic: a shared object

$ gcc main.o -lutil          # CORRECT: libraries AFTER the objects that need them
$ gcc -lutil main.o          # WRONG: at -lutil nothing is undefined yet, so nothing is pulled
$ gcc -Wl,--start-group -la -lb -Wl,--end-group   # for mutual dependencies

$ ldd ./app                  # which shared objects it needs at load time
$ readelf -d ./app | grep -E 'NEEDED|RPATH|RUNPATH'
$ nm -D --undefined-only ./app

concepts.L1: A static library is an archive the linker extracts from selectively at build time; a shared library is a separate file resolved at load time. Static linking duplicates code into every binary; dynamic linking shares one copy and allows independent upgrades.
concepts.L2: Link order matters for static archives and not for object files. The linker keeps a set of currently undefined symbols and scans each input once, so a library listed before its users contributes nothing - the classic 'undefined reference' where the library is clearly on the command line.
concepts.L3: The traditional Unix linker makes one left-to-right pass, keeping a set of undefined symbols. An object file is always included; an archive member only if it defines a symbol currently in that set. So `gcc -lm main.o` reaches libm with nothing undefined, extracts nothing, then finds `sin` undefined with no archives left. --start-group re-scans until a fixed point, at a cost. Shared libraries behave differently: the link records a NEEDED entry and defers resolution to ld.so, so order matters less at build time and more at run time, where the search path (RUNPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, ldconfig) decides which copy loads and interposition decides which definition wins.

L4.prompt_tpl: `gcc -lm calc.o -o calc` reports 'undefined reference to `{f}`' while `gcc calc.o -lm -o calc` succeeds. Explain the mechanism.
L4.answer: The linker scans inputs left to right, extracting an archive member only if it resolves a symbol that is undefined at that moment. When it reaches -lm nothing is undefined yet, so no member is extracted; calc.o then introduces the undefined reference with no archives remaining. Placing -lm after calc.o gives the linker the undefined symbol before it scans the archive.
L4.explanation: This is a one-pass algorithm chosen for speed in the 1970s and preserved for compatibility. Modern lld behaves the same way by default.

L4.prompt_tpl: A container image ships {n} services, each statically linked. Give one advantage and two costs versus dynamic linking.
L4.answer: Advantage: each binary is self-contained, so there is no runtime dependency resolution, no version skew, faster startup and no ld.so search. Costs: every binary carries its own copy of every library, so image size and page cache footprint multiply; and a security fix in a library requires rebuilding and redeploying every binary rather than replacing one .so.
L4.explanation: The page-cache point is the one people miss: dynamically linked processes share one copy of libc's text pages in memory, statically linked ones do not.

void foo(double);       //             _Z3food

concepts.L1: C++ encodes parameter types, namespaces and qualifiers into the linker symbol, so overloads get distinct names. extern "C" turns that off for a declaration, producing a plain C symbol that any language's FFI can bind.
concepts.L2: extern "C" affects the symbol name only - the calling convention is the platform's either way. What it does change is that you can have at most one such function per name, so an overload set cannot be exported, and neither can a template or a member function.
concepts.L3: The linker matches by string, so a language with overloading must encode the signature into the string; the Itanium scheme is a compact grammar (_Z, nested name, parameter type codes) that also encodes const, references and template arguments, hence the long names. This is a real type-safety mechanism across translation units: change a parameter type and the mangled name changes, so a stale caller fails at link time instead of corrupting the stack the way C does. It is also why C++ ABI stability is hard - adding a member or bumping the standard library's inline namespace changes names or layouts and breaks binary compatibility. Every cross-language FFI therefore narrows to a C surface.

L4.prompt_tpl: A C++ file defines `void {f}(int)` and a C file calls `{f}(3)`. The link fails with 'undefined reference to `{f}`'. Why, and what is the one-line fix?
L4.answer: The C++ definition emitted the mangled symbol _Z4initi (or similar), while the C caller emits an undefined reference to the plain name `init`. Declare the C++ definition `extern "C" void init(int);` so it emits the unmangled symbol.
L4.explanation: Confirm with `nm -C` on both objects: one shows the mangled T symbol, the other a plain U. This is the entire content of most FFI link failures.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why can a C++ library export a {n}-overload function set to C++ callers but not to C or Python's ctypes?
L4.answer: Overloads are distinguished only by mangled names, and mangling is a C++ ABI detail that C has no notion of - a C caller can only name a plain symbol, and only one function may own each plain name. Exporting to C means choosing distinct names (init_int, init_double) inside extern "C" wrappers.
L4.explanation: This is why every C++ library with a C API ships a hand-written flat wrapper layer, and why pybind11 and cffi exist to generate the equivalent.

; int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }   on Linux x86-64
add:
    lea   eax, [rdi + rsi]      ; a in edi, b in esi, result in eax
    ret

; Integer/pointer args:  rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9   then the stack (right to left)
; Float args:            xmm0 - xmm7
; Return:                rax (and rdx for 128-bit), xmm0 for floating point
; Callee-saved:          rbx, rbp, r12-r15, rsp     - everything else is caller-saved
; Stack: 16-byte aligned at the call;  128-byte RED ZONE below rsp for leaf functions
; Varargs: al holds the number of vector registers used
L0.cloze:

; The return value comes back in {{c2::rax}}.
; {{c3::Callee}}-saved registers (rbx, rbp, r12-r15) must be preserved across a call.
; The stack must be {{c4::16}}-byte aligned at the point of the call instruction.

concepts.L1: A calling convention fixes which registers carry arguments and return values, who preserves what, and how the stack is aligned. System V AMD64 is the Linux/macOS convention; Windows x64 differs, which is why object files are not portable between them.
concepts.L2: Structs are not passed as a unit: the ABI classifies each 8-byte chunk as INTEGER, SSE or MEMORY, so a two-word struct arrives in two registers while a three-word one is copied to the stack. That threshold is why adding one field to a small struct can measurably slow a hot call.
concepts.L3: The ABI is the contract that makes separate compilation and cross-language calls possible: because it is fixed, a Rust caller and a C callee agree without either compiler knowing the other exists. Register-based argument passing is the reason a small function call costs a few cycles rather than a memory round trip, and the callee-saved list is why a leaf function can use rax, rcx and rdx freely without saving anything. The red zone - 128 bytes below rsp that signal handlers must not clobber - lets leaf functions use scratch space with no stack adjustment at all, which is why kernels compile with -mno-red-zone. Reading a disassembly is largely a matter of knowing this table by heart.

L4.prompt_tpl: For `long f(long a, long b, long c, long d, long e, long g, long h)` on System V AMD64, where do arguments {k} and 7 arrive?
L4.answer: Arguments 1-6 go in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9 in that order - so argument 1 is rdi, 3 is rdx, 6 is r9. The seventh is pushed onto the stack and read at [rsp+8] inside the callee (after the return address).
L4.explanation: This is why functions with more than six integer parameters are measurably more expensive, and one argument for grouping parameters into a struct passed by pointer.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why does the same C source compiled on Linux and on Windows produce object files that cannot be linked together, even for the same CPU?
L4.answer: They use different calling conventions (rdi/rsi/rdx/rcx/r8/r9 versus rcx/rdx/r8/r9 with a 32-byte shadow space), different callee-saved register sets, different struct-passing rules, and different object formats (ELF versus PE/COFF) and name decoration. A call compiled for one convention reads its arguments from the wrong registers under the other.
L4.explanation: Same ISA, different ABI. This is the cleanest demonstration that an ABI is a separate layer from the instruction set.

concepts.t: Dynamic loading: PLT, GOT, dlopen, and symbol interposition
concepts.L1: Calls into a shared library are indirected through the PLT and GOT so the dynamic linker can bind them at load time or on first call. Because binding searches objects in load order, the first definition of a name wins for the whole process.
concepts.L2: Interposition applies to a library's calls to its own functions too, unless it was built with -fvisibility=hidden or -Bsymbolic. That is why LD_PRELOAD can replace malloc for all of libc, and also why an accidental symbol clash between two libraries silently redirects one library's internal calls into the other's code.
concepts.L3: Position-independent code holds no absolute addresses, so a call to an external function jumps to a PLT stub, which jumps through a GOT slot. At first call the slot points into the resolver, which searches objects in load order, writes the address into the GOT and jumps there; later calls are one extra indirect jump. The search is what creates interposition: the executable first, then LD_PRELOADed objects, then each NEEDED library in order. That makes profilers, allocators and sanitisers work without recompiling, and makes symbol collisions dangerous. Full RELRO plus LD_BIND_NOW resolves everything at startup and makes the GOT read-only, trading a slower start for one fewer attack surface.

L4.prompt_tpl: How does an LD_PRELOADed malloc replacement intercept allocations made INSIDE libc, given libc was compiled long before your library existed?
L4.answer: libc's internal calls to malloc also go through its PLT and are resolved by the dynamic linker at run time, searching objects in load order. LD_PRELOAD places your object ahead of libc, so the resolver binds those slots to your definition. Nothing about libc is recompiled or patched - the indirection was always there.
L4.explanation: It also explains the exceptions: calls libc makes to hidden-visibility internal aliases, or a library built with -Bsymbolic, bind internally and cannot be interposed.

L4.prompt_tpl: An interposing library defines `malloc` and calls `printf` inside it for logging. The program hangs or crashes at startup on {n} of the machines. Diagnose.
L4.answer: printf allocates, so it calls malloc, which re-enters your interposer - infinite recursion, or a deadlock if the allocator's lock is not reentrant. It is also unsafe before dlsym has resolved the real malloc, since dlsym itself may allocate. Use a static bootstrap buffer for early allocations and write logs with the raw write syscall.
L4.explanation: This is the standard hazard of interposing an allocator, and the reason production allocator shims are so careful about their own dependencies.

INT_MIN / -1;                  /* UB - and on x86 idiv raises SIGFPE                     */

/* Defences */
gcc -fwrapv           /* define it as two's-complement wraparound                        */
gcc -ftrapv           /* trap at run time                                                */
gcc -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow      /* report it with file and line              */
if (__builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &r)) { /* handle */ }   /* the portable checked add     */

concepts.L1: Signed overflow has no defined result, so the compiler assumes it never happens and reasons with unbounded integers. Unsigned arithmetic is specified modulo 2^N, which makes it well defined and, for the same reason, harder to optimise.
concepts.L2: The optimiser uses the assumption to widen loop counters to 64 bits, to prove `i + 1 > i`, and to hoist bounds checks - so an overflow does not merely produce a wrapped value, it deletes the code that would have caught it. INT_MIN / -1 goes further and raises SIGFPE on x86.
concepts.L3: The rule exists so that a compiler may treat `int` as a mathematical integer: it can widen a 32-bit loop counter to 64 bits without materialising wraparound, fold `x*2/2` to `x`, prove induction variables monotonic, and vectorise loops whose trip count depends on one. All of that is invalid for unsigned, which is why unsigned loop counters can generate worse code despite being safer. Violations are unpredictable in the strict sense: gcc may keep the wrap at -O0, fold the comparison at -O2, and turn a bounded loop infinite at -O3, from one source. Use -fwrapv when you need wrapping semantics, and the __builtin_*_overflow intrinsics when you need to detect it.

L4.prompt_tpl: `int i; for (i = 0; i <= {n}; i++) count++;` where {n} is INT_MAX. What does the loop do at -O0 and at -O2?
L4.answer: At -O0 the counter wraps to INT_MIN, the condition i <= INT_MAX stays true, and the loop never terminates - with UB on every wrap. At -O2 the compiler may prove from no-overflow that i <= INT_MAX always holds and emit an unconditional infinite loop, or widen i to 64 bits and terminate. Both are permitted; neither is a bug in the compiler.
L4.explanation: Any answer that asserts one specific behaviour is wrong. The right response is that the program has no defined meaning and must be rewritten with an unsigned or wider counter.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need to detect whether `a + b` overflows for ints a={a}, b={b}. Why is `if (a + b < a)` wrong, and what is right?
L4.answer: The test itself performs the overflowing addition, which is UB, and the compiler may then delete the comparison as provably false. Correct options: __builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &r), or a check that avoids the overflow (b > 0 ? a > INT_MAX - b : a < INT_MIN - b), or do the arithmetic in a wider type.
L4.explanation: The trick that works for unsigned - test the wrapped result - is exactly what is unavailable for signed, because there is no defined wrapped result to test.

concepts.L1: Strict aliasing lets the compiler assume that pointers to unrelated types never refer to the same object, so a store through a float* cannot affect a value cached from an int*. Violating it is UB and the symptom is a stale value, not a crash.
concepts.L2: memcpy is the correct pun and it is not slow: every mainstream compiler turns a fixed-size memcpy between scalars into a single move instruction. The cast version is both undefined and, at -O2, capable of producing a value the memory never held, because the reload was optimised away.
concepts.L3: The rule is an aliasing oracle for the optimiser. Without it, every store through any pointer would force a reload of every value held in a register, and no non-trivial loop over two pointer arguments could be vectorised. With it, `void f(int* a, float* b)` may keep *a in a register across a store to *b. The failure mode is therefore a stale read rather than a fault, and it appears only at optimisation levels where the value was cached - which is exactly why the bug shows up when a project moves from -O0 to -O2, or upgrades its compiler. The character-type exception exists so that memcpy, serialisation and hashing remain expressible; that is also why memcpy is the sanctioned pun.

L4.prompt_tpl: The fast inverse square root trick `i = *(long*)&y; i = 0x5f3759df - (i>>1); y = *(float*)&i;` is compiled at -O2 with a modern gcc. What is wrong and what is the modern spelling?
L4.answer: Both casts violate strict aliasing: a float object is read through a long lvalue and vice versa. The compiler may keep y in a register across the integer store and produce a stale result, and gcc warns with -Wstrict-aliasing. The modern spelling is memcpy in both directions, or std::bit_cast in C++20, which generates the same instructions with defined semantics.
L4.explanation: The original Quake III code predates the rule being enforced. It still 'works' in many builds, which is what keeps it circulating.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is memcpy between a float and an int{n} not slower than the pointer cast?
L4.answer: For a compile-time-constant size matching a register width, the compiler lowers memcpy to a single load or move - there is no library call and no copy loop. Godbolt shows both versions producing the same one or two instructions, so the defined version costs nothing.
L4.explanation: This is worth verifying yourself once. The belief that memcpy is expensive is the main reason people keep writing the undefined version.

concepts.t: Use-after-free, dangling references, and lifetime UB

L0.cloze:
/* An object's {{c1::lifetime}} ends at the closing brace (automatic), at delete/free
   (dynamic), or when a container {{c2::reallocates}}.
   Using any pointer or reference to it afterwards is {{c3::undefined}}, not "reads garbage".
   The tool that finds it with both allocation and free stacks is {{c4::AddressSanitizer}}. */

concepts.L1: A pointer or reference is valid only within the referent's lifetime. Using one afterwards is UB - the storage may be reused, poisoned, or unmapped, and the compiler may assume the access never happens.
concepts.L2: Container invalidation is the version people forget: push_back may reallocate, so every pointer, reference and iterator into a vector is invalidated by one insertion. std::string_view and std::span make it worse by looking like values while borrowing, so binding one to a temporary dangles at the end of the full expression.
concepts.L3: Lifetime UB is dangerous precisely because the memory usually still reads back plausibly: freed heap blocks retain their bytes until reused, and a dead stack frame is overwritten only by the next call, so the bug appears intermittently or after an unrelated change. ASan makes it deterministic by poisoning freed regions with redzones and quarantining them so the address is not reused immediately, and reports the allocation, free and use stacks together. Vector invalidation follows from growth: exceeding capacity allocates a new buffer, moves the elements and frees the old, so an interior pointer taken earlier points into freed storage. reserve() up front, or indices, avoid it.

L4.prompt_tpl: `std::vector<int> v; v.push_back({a}); int& r = v[0]; for (int i = 0; i < {n}; i++) v.push_back(i); std::cout << r;` What is wrong, and give two fixes.
L4.answer: The pushes exceed capacity and reallocate, so r refers to the freed buffer - use-after-free, and the printed value is whatever survives there. Fix by calling v.reserve(n+1) before taking the reference so no reallocation occurs, or by using the index (v[0]) at the point of use rather than holding a reference.
L4.explanation: ASan reports it as heap-use-after-free with the reallocation's free stack. Without ASan it usually prints the right answer, because the freed block is often untouched.

L4.prompt_tpl: `std::string_view sv = std::string("{s}") + "x"; std::cout << sv;` What is the defect?
L4.answer: The temporary string produced by the concatenation is destroyed at the end of the full expression, so sv points into freed memory before it is ever used. Unlike a const reference, a string_view does not extend a temporary's lifetime. Assign to a std::string, or keep the owning object alive in a named variable.
L4.explanation: This is the standard string_view/span trap: they are borrow types with value syntax, and nothing in the declaration hints that the right-hand side must outlive them.

L0.cloze:
/* {{c1::Undefined}}: the whole program has no meaning; the optimiser may assume it
   cannot happen.
   {{c2::Unspecified}}: one of several valid behaviours, not documented.
   {{c3::Implementation-defined}}: one of several valid behaviours, and it must be
   {{c4::documented}}.
   Only the first is a bug the compiler is licensed to exploit against you. */

concepts.L1: Three distinct categories. Undefined behaviour removes all requirements on the program. Unspecified behaviour picks from a set of valid options with no documentation obligation. Implementation-defined behaviour picks from that set and must document the choice.
concepts.L2: Depending on unspecified behaviour gives you a portability bug; depending on undefined behaviour gives you a program the optimiser may transform arbitrarily, including deleting code that runs before it. Sorting your program's surprises into these three buckets is the difference between a porting task and a security incident.
concepts.L3: The categories divide the standard's silence into three levels of licence. Implementation-defined items (sizeof(int), char's signedness, size_t's width) are portability parameters: query them with limits.h or numeric_limits. Unspecified items (argument evaluation order, padding byte values) mean the program has several correct executions and you must not depend on one. Undefined behaviour is categorically different because it is a premise, not an outcome: the standard permits the compiler to assume it does not occur, and the transformations that follow are not limited to the offending expression. That is why sanitisers exist for the third category and mere warnings for the first two.

L4.prompt_tpl: Classify each: (a) `printf("%d %d", i++, i++)`, (b) `sizeof(long)`, (c) `1 << {k}` for a 32-bit int, (d) the value of an uninitialised local read as an int.
L4.answer: (a) In C the two modifications of i are unsequenced, so it is undefined; the argument evaluation ORDER alone is unspecified, but the double modification makes it UB. (b) implementation-defined - 8 on LP64, 4 on Windows LLP64. (c) 1<<31 is UB in C (the result is not representable in int; it is defined in C++20); 1<<32 is UB in both, shifting by at least the width. (d) UB in practice - the value is indeterminate, and reading one can yield a trap representation or different values on successive reads.
L4.explanation: The distinction between (a)'s order being unspecified and the expression being undefined is the crux: unspecified order plus two modifications is what crosses the line. C++17 changed some of these sequencing rules, which is why the language version must be stated.

L4.prompt_tpl: Why is 'the compiler may do anything' a fair description of UB but a poor description of unspecified behaviour?
L4.answer: For unspecified behaviour the standard still bounds the outcome to a set of valid choices, and the rest of the program keeps its meaning - the result differs across implementations but the execution remains defined. UB imposes no requirement on the entire execution, so the compiler may assume the path is unreachable and delete surrounding code, including operations sequenced before it.
L4.explanation: This is why the correct response to unspecified behaviour is 'do not depend on it' and the correct response to UB is 'remove it'.

concepts.t: std::atomic in practice: load, store, fetch_add, and the memory_order argument
concepts.L1: std::atomic makes an operation indivisible and, through its memory_order argument, controls what surrounding non-atomic accesses may be reordered across it. The default is seq_cst, which is always correct and usually stronger than needed.
concepts.L2: atomic<T> for a large T is not lock-free: the library falls back to a hidden mutex, so a lock-free algorithm built on it is neither lock-free nor faster. is_lock_free() is a run-time query and is_always_lock_free a compile-time one - assert on it.
concepts.L3: An atomic load or store on a naturally aligned, machine-word-sized object is just a mov on x86; the atomicity comes from the hardware, and the memory_order argument controls what the compiler and CPU may reorder around it, not the instruction itself. Read-modify-write operations are different: they compile to a lock-prefixed instruction (lock xadd for fetch_add) that acquires the cache line exclusively for the duration, costing 20-50 cycles uncontended and far more when several cores fight for the line. That is why a shared atomic counter scales badly - it is not the atomicity but the coherence traffic on one line - and why per-thread counters summed on read are the standard fix.

L4.prompt_tpl: {t} threads each run `for (int i = 0; i < {n}; i++) c++;` where c is `std::atomic<int>` with relaxed ordering. What is the final value, and what if c were a plain int? Answer with the final value of the atomic counter.
L4.answer: With std::atomic and relaxed ordering the final value is exactly t*n: relaxed still guarantees the RMW is indivisible, so no increment is lost. With a plain int it is a data race - UB in C++ - and in practice a value well below t*n.
L4.explanation: Relaxed removes ordering guarantees about OTHER memory, never atomicity of the operation itself. This is the single most common misreading of relaxed.

L4.prompt_tpl: A profile shows {p}% of cycles inside `counter.fetch_add(1, relaxed)` shared by {t} threads. The atomic is already relaxed. What now?
L4.answer: Shard the counter: one padded, alignas(64) counter per thread, summed when the value is read
L4.explanation: Java's LongAdder is exactly this design, and it is why it beats AtomicLong by an order of magnitude under contention while being slower for a single thread.
options: Shard the counter: one padded, alignas(64) counter per thread, summed when the value is read
Raise the ordering to seq_cst so the hardware can coalesce increments into one cache-line transfer
Replace the atomic with a plain int under a mutex, since an uncontended mutex is cheaper than a locked RMW

concepts.t: compare_exchange_weak vs strong, and the CAS loop
concepts.L1: compare_exchange atomically swaps in a new value if the current one matches expected, and otherwise loads the actual value into expected. weak may fail spuriously; strong may not, at the cost of an internal retry loop on LL/SC machines.
concepts.L2: The parameter is an in-out reference, so the retry loop needs no reload - and any recomputation of the desired value must happen inside the loop, using the updated expected. Recomputing outside the loop is the classic bug: the update is then based on a stale value and silently overwrites another thread's work.
concepts.L3: On x86, compare_exchange compiles to lock cmpxchg, which cannot fail spuriously, so weak and strong generate identical code. On ARM and POWER the primitive is load-linked/store-conditional: the store fails if anything wrote the line since the load, including an unrelated variable in the same line or a context switch. weak exposes that failure directly; strong wraps it in an internal loop, which is wasted work if you are already looping. Hence the rule: weak inside a retry loop, strong for a single conclusive attempt. The two memory orders are separate because the failure path performed no store and needs no release; passing seq_cst for both is a common and needless cost.

L4.answer: desired is computed once, from the initial expected. On a failed exchange, expected is updated to the current value but desired is not recomputed, so the loop eventually writes a value derived from a stale reading - clobbering every concurrent update. The recomputation must be inside the loop body.
L4.explanation: It usually passes tests under low contention, because the first attempt succeeds. This is the standard CAS-loop defect.

L4.prompt_tpl: You need one conditional update, not a loop: set a flag from 0 to {v} only if it is still 0. weak or strong?
L4.answer: strong: with no surrounding loop there is nothing to absorb a spurious failure, and you would misread it as losing the race
L4.explanation: On x86 the choice generates the same instruction, so the bug is invisible there and appears on ARM - the standard shape of a portability defect in lock-free code.
options: strong: with no surrounding loop there is nothing to absorb a spurious failure, and you would misread it as losing the race
weak: it lowers to a single instruction everywhere, and a failure simply means the flag was no longer 0
Either: spurious failure can only happen when the comparison genuinely fails, so outside a loop they are interchangeable

concepts.t: Mutexes in code: lock_guard, unique_lock, and what a lock costs
concepts.L1: A mutex on Linux is an atomic word plus a futex: the fast path is one compare-exchange in user space, and the kernel is involved only when a thread must actually block. Always acquire through an RAII guard.
concepts.L2: The received wisdom that 'locks are slow' is about contention, not locking. An uncontended acquire is roughly the cost of an atomic increment; a contended one is three orders of magnitude more, because it costs a syscall, a context switch and a scheduler wakeup. Reduce contention before replacing the lock.
concepts.L3: glibc's pthread_mutex holds a state word; locking does a compare-exchange from unlocked to locked, and on success returns immediately - so an uncontended lock costs about as much as the atomic RMW under it. On failure it may spin briefly, then calls futex(FUTEX_WAIT) to sleep on the address; unlock sees waiters and calls FUTEX_WAKE. So the cost distribution is bimodal, and averages are useless. The design implications follow directly: shrink critical sections, shard the data so threads take different locks, and prefer scoped_lock when taking several, since its ordering algorithm prevents the two-mutex deadlock a hand-written pair invites.

L4.prompt_tpl: Thread A does `lock(m1); lock(m2);` and thread B does `lock(m2); lock(m1);` with a {ms} ms critical section. What happens, and give two fixes.
L4.answer: Deadlock: A holds m1 waiting for m2 while B holds m2 waiting for m1, and neither can proceed. Fixes: impose a global lock order so every thread takes m1 before m2, or use std::scoped_lock(m1, m2), which applies a deadlock-avoiding algorithm (try-and-back-off) regardless of the order written.
L4.explanation: The longer the critical section, the more likely the interleaving, but the bug exists at any duration. TSan detects lock-order inversions even when they do not deadlock during the run.

L4.prompt_tpl: A critical section is {ns} ns long and is entered {n} million times per second across {t} threads. Estimate whether contention dominates, and say what you would change first.
L4.answer: Total time inside the lock per second = ns * n * 1e6 nanoseconds. If that exceeds 1e9 ns (one second of serialised work) the lock is saturated and adding threads cannot help. For 5000 ns at 1e6 entries/s that is 5 seconds of work per second - hopeless; for 50 ns at 1e6 it is 0.05 s, only 5% serialised. Shrink the critical section first, then shard the lock.
L4.explanation: This is Amdahl applied to a lock: the serial fraction is the fraction of wall time the lock is held. Compute it before choosing a lock-free replacement.
